flashcards.back: A first-party, fully managed file storage service built on NetApp technology, offering NFS (v3 and v4.1), SMB, and dual-protocol volumes with low latency at the higher service levels, snapshots, cross-region replication, and volumes sized by capacity pool quota. It targets enterprise file workloads such as SAP, HPC, and lift-and-shift of NAS applications.
flashcards.detail: Look for requirements such as migrating NetApp workloads, very low latency for file access, or enterprise NAS features that Azure Files does not match.

flashcards.back: A managed storage area network service that lets you provision one SAN with pooled capacity and performance and carve it into volumes that connect over iSCSI to many compute resources, including VMs, AKS, and Azure VMware Solution. You scale base capacity, IOPS, and throughput of the SAN as a whole rather than per disk.
flashcards.detail: A requirement to consolidate block storage for many workloads under one pooled, scalable resource points to Elastic SAN rather than separately sized managed disks.

flashcards.back: A unified software-as-a-service analytics platform that brings data engineering, data integration (Data Factory), data warehousing, real-time intelligence, data science, and Power BI into one workspace on OneLake, a single logical data lake for the whole organization. Shortcuts reference data in other locations without copying it, and Fabric items store data in open Delta Parquet format.
flashcards.detail: A design that wants one governed platform for ingest, lake, warehouse, and reporting, with little infrastructure to manage, points to Fabric.

flashcards.front: Choosing a data analysis platform: Fabric, Databricks, and Synapse
flashcards.back: Microsoft Fabric is the integrated SaaS analytics platform. Azure Databricks is a Spark-based platform for data engineering and machine learning with notebooks, Delta Lake, and a rich ecosystem, and teams often keep it for existing Spark workloads. Azure Synapse Analytics is the earlier analytics service with dedicated and serverless SQL pools and Spark pools, still available for existing solutions.
flashcards.detail: A new analytics estate with low operational overhead leans to Fabric. An existing Spark and MLOps investment leans to Databricks.

flashcards.front: Azure Stream Analytics vs. Event Hubs vs. Fabric Real-Time Intelligence
flashcards.back: Event Hubs ingests and buffers high-volume event streams. Azure Stream Analytics is a fully managed engine that runs continuous SQL-like queries, with time windows, over streams from Event Hubs or IoT Hub and writes results to stores such as SQL Database, Power BI, or Blob Storage. Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric provides event streams and real-time analytics inside the Fabric platform.
flashcards.detail: Ingestion is Event Hubs, continuous processing is Stream Analytics, and storing the results for later analysis is a different service again.

flashcards.front: Balancing storage features, performance, and cost
flashcards.back: Cost levers for Azure Storage include the redundancy level, the access tier (Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive), lifecycle management that moves data between tiers automatically, reserved capacity for predictable volumes (a one-year or three-year commitment), and Standard or Premium performance. Premium block blob accounts, Premium file shares, and Ultra or Premium SSD v2 disks buy low latency and high IOPS at higher cost.
flashcards.detail: A workload with a long-lived, predictable footprint adds reserved capacity. A data set with decaying access adds lifecycle rules.

flashcards.back: Azure Storage designs for at least 11 nines of durability over a year with locally redundant storage, at least 12 nines with zone-redundant storage, and at least 16 nines with geo-redundant or geo-zone-redundant storage. Durability is about not losing data, while availability, and an SLA, is about being able to read and write it, so read-access variants add availability from the secondary region.
flashcards.detail: A requirement for the highest durability and protection against a regional loss points to GRS or GZRS. Surviving a zone failure alone needs only ZRS.

flashcards.front: Backup and recovery for compute workloads
flashcards.back: Azure Backup protects Azure VMs with snapshots plus a copy in a Recovery Services vault, and protects SQL Server and SAP HANA databases running in VMs with workload-aware backups. On-premises servers use the MARS agent, Azure Backup Server, or System Center DPM. For VM, scale set, and hybrid workloads that must resume within a tight recovery time objective rather than restore from a backup, Azure Site Recovery replication is the better fit.
flashcards.detail: Backup answers 'restore an earlier copy'. Site Recovery answers 'run the workload somewhere else, soon'.

flashcards.back: Azure SQL Database takes automated backups with point-in-time restore, kept for 7 days by default and configurable from 1 to 35 days, and long-term retention can keep full backups for up to 10 years. Azure Cosmos DB offers periodic backup, or continuous backup with point-in-time restore within a 7-, 30-, or 35-day tier. SQL Server in a VM uses Azure Backup's workload backup, and flexible server databases keep their own automated backups.
flashcards.detail: 'Restore to any point in the last N days' points to point-in-time restore or continuous backup. 'Keep yearly copies for seven years' points to long-term retention.

flashcards.front: Backup and recovery for unstructured data: Blob Storage and Azure Files
flashcards.back: For blobs, operational backup is continuous, keeps changes inside the source storage account, and restores to a point in time; vaulted backup copies data to a Backup vault in a separate, Microsoft-managed location, protecting against account deletion or malicious deletion. Azure Files can be backed up through a Recovery Services vault using snapshot backups, or with the vaulted tier that copies data out of the storage account.
flashcards.detail: A requirement to survive deletion of the whole storage account rules out options that keep the data only inside that account, such as soft delete, versioning, snapshots, and operational backup.

flashcards.front: Protecting backups from ransomware and insider deletion
flashcards.back: An immutable vault blocks operations that could lead to the loss of recovery points, and locking the setting makes it irreversible. Soft delete retains deleted backup data, and enhanced soft delete makes the retention period configurable and can be made always on. Multi-user authorization uses a Resource Guard, owned by a separate team or in another subscription or tenant, so critical operations need a second approver. Cross Region Restore lets you restore from the paired region.
flashcards.detail: A compromised backup administrator is the threat model behind immutability, enhanced soft delete, and Resource Guard.

flashcards.front: Azure Site Recovery for Azure, on-premises, and other workloads
flashcards.back: Site Recovery replicates Azure VMs between regions, on-premises VMware VMs, Hyper-V VMs, and physical servers to Azure, and Windows instances from AWS to Azure. Failover is orchestrated with recovery plans that order the start-up of tiers and add scripts or manual steps, and a test failover validates the plan in an isolated network without affecting production.
flashcards.detail: A hybrid disaster recovery requirement with a minutes-level recovery time and no secondary datacenter to build points to Site Recovery with Azure as the target.

flashcards.front: High availability for compute: SLAs and placement
flashcards.back: Two or more VMs spread across availability zones qualify for a 99.99 percent SLA, VMs in an availability set within one datacenter for 99.95 percent, and a single VM with premium storage for 99.9 percent. Virtual Machine Scale Sets spread instances across zones and fault domains automatically. In front of them, zone-redundant load balancers and application gateways keep the entry point available when a zone fails.
flashcards.detail: Zones protect against a datacenter failure. Availability sets protect against a rack or host failure inside one datacenter. Neither protects against a regional outage.

flashcards.back: Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance can be zone-redundant so that a zone failure is handled by automatic failover inside the region with no application change, while auto-failover groups add a regional secondary with a single listener endpoint. PostgreSQL and MySQL flexible servers offer zone-redundant high availability with a synchronously replicated standby in another zone. SQL Server on VMs uses Always On availability groups across zones.
flashcards.detail: Zone redundancy answers a datacenter failure inside a region. A failover group answers the loss of the entire region.

flashcards.front: High availability for semi-structured and unstructured data
flashcards.back: Zone-redundant storage keeps data available through a zone failure, and geo-zone-redundant storage adds a secondary region, with the read-access variants allowing reads from it. Azure Files and managed disks support zone-redundant options. Azure Cosmos DB can be deployed across availability zones and across regions with multi-region writes and automatic failover priorities.
flashcards.detail: Cosmos DB availability is configured by adding regions and zones to the account, and the consistency level chosen affects what multi-region writes allow.

flashcards.back: The global tier of Azure Load Balancer places one static anycast public IP address in front of regional Standard public load balancers. Traffic goes to the closest healthy regional deployment using geo-proximity routing, and fails over to the next best region if one becomes unhealthy. It works at layer 4 for TCP and UDP and preserves the client IP address.
flashcards.detail: For HTTP applications that need path routing, caching, or WAF, Azure Front Door is the global choice; for any TCP or UDP traffic, the global load balancer fits.

flashcards.back: Resiliency in Azure, the new name of the Azure Business Continuity Center, is a unified place to manage the resilience posture of the whole estate: backup and disaster recovery protection across Azure Backup and Site Recovery, zone resiliency, and ransomware protection. It shows protected and unprotected resources across subscriptions in one view.
flashcards.detail: Older material may say Business Continuity Center or Backup center. Backup center is the legacy experience that it replaced.

flashcards.front: Azure Batch and CycleCloud for batch and HPC compute
flashcards.back: Azure Batch is a managed service for running large-scale parallel and high-performance computing jobs: you define pools of compute nodes, jobs, and tasks, and Batch schedules the tasks, scales the pool, and can use Spot VMs to cut cost. There is no charge for Batch itself, only for the underlying resources. Azure CycleCloud orchestrates traditional HPC clusters with schedulers such as Slurm.
flashcards.detail: Embarrassingly parallel work such as rendering, simulations, or nightly processing of many files points to Batch. A scheduler-based cluster that scientists already know points to CycleCloud.

flashcards.front: Choosing a VM-based solution: pricing and placement options
flashcards.back: Spot VMs use spare capacity at a deep discount but can be evicted, so they suit interruptible work. Reservations and savings plans lower the cost of steady usage for one or three years. Azure Dedicated Host gives single-tenant physical servers for compliance or per-core licensing. Azure Compute Gallery shares versioned images across regions and subscriptions. Proximity placement groups keep VMs physically close for low latency.
flashcards.detail: Interruptible means Spot, steady and predictable means reservations, and a physical-server isolation or licensing requirement means Dedicated Host.

flashcards.back: Confidential computing protects data in use by running workloads in a hardware-based trusted execution environment, so that even the host and cloud operators cannot read memory. Confidential VMs offer this for lift-and-shift of whole VMs on hardware such as AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX, and keys can be released only to an attested workload using secure key release with Managed HSM.
flashcards.detail: Encryption at rest and in transit are already standard. 'Protect data while it is being processed' is the signal for confidential computing.

flashcards.back: A first-party Azure service that runs a VMware vSphere, vSAN, and NSX private cloud on dedicated bare-metal hosts in Azure. Workloads can move without conversion or re-IP using the same VMware tools, which suits datacenter exits on a deadline or applications that cannot be re-platformed, while Azure services can be added around it.
flashcards.detail: A fast datacenter exit that keeps VMware skills and tooling points to Azure VMware Solution rather than rehosting each VM as a native Azure VM.

flashcards.back: A single-tenant deployment of App Service that is injected into your virtual network and uses the Isolated v2 pricing tiers, giving network isolation, dedicated compute, and very high scale. It suits applications with strict isolation, compliance, or private-only requirements, at higher cost than the multitenant service.
flashcards.detail: A web workload that must run in a dedicated, VNet-injected environment points to an App Service Environment. Regional VNet integration only covers outbound calls.

flashcards.front: Azure Static Web Apps and Logic Apps hosting options
flashcards.back: Azure Static Web Apps hosts static front ends and builds them from a GitHub or Azure DevOps repository, with globally distributed content and serverless API back ends. Logic Apps comes as Consumption (multitenant, pay per execution) or Standard (single-tenant runtime with multiple workflows per app, virtual network integration, and local development).
flashcards.detail: A requirement for private networking or predictable pricing for many workflows points to Logic Apps Standard. Occasional, low-volume workflows suit Consumption.

flashcards.front: Service Bus queues vs. Storage queues
flashcards.back: Storage queues are simple and cheap, suit queues that stay below 80 GB, and are used with the standard Storage SDKs. Service Bus is chosen for guaranteed first-in-first-out ordering with sessions, automatic duplicate detection, dead-letter queues, transactions, topics and subscriptions for publish and subscribe, AMQP 1.0, and, in the Premium tier, messages up to 100 MB.
flashcards.detail: A queue that needs ordering, duplicate detection, or a dead-letter queue is Service Bus. A simple work queue of small messages is a Storage queue.

flashcards.front: Event Hubs and Event Grid design features
flashcards.back: Event Hubs ingests streams through partitions that consumer groups read independently, can capture events automatically to Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage, and exposes a Kafka-compatible endpoint. Event Grid routes discrete events to handlers with filtering, retries, and dead-lettering, supports the MQTT and HTTP protocols, and offers system topics for Azure service events.
flashcards.detail: Existing Kafka producers pointing at Azure points to Event Hubs. Reacting to 'a blob was created' with a function points to Event Grid.

flashcards.front: Cloud design patterns for resilient applications
flashcards.back: Cache-Aside loads data into a cache on demand. Queue-Based Load Leveling buffers bursts, and Competing Consumers lets several workers drain a queue. Claim Check passes a reference to large payloads instead of the data. Retry handles transient faults, Circuit Breaker stops calls to a failing dependency, and Bulkhead isolates resources so one failure does not spread. CQRS separates reads from writes, Saga manages distributed transactions, and Strangler Fig migrates a system gradually.
flashcards.detail: A scenario that describes a failure mode is usually asking for the pattern that names it: transient faults, cascading failure, bursts, or oversized messages.

flashcards.front: Azure API Management tiers and gateways
flashcards.back: API Management is offered in Consumption (serverless, pay per call), Developer (non-production), Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers, plus the v2 tiers (Basic v2, Standard v2, Premium v2). Network and scale features differ by tier: Premium and Premium v2 support virtual network injection, and Premium supports multi-region deployment. A self-hosted gateway can run in other environments, including on-premises, while being managed from the Azure instance.
flashcards.detail: Developer has no SLA and is for evaluation. A requirement for a gateway close to on-premises backends points to the self-hosted gateway.

flashcards.front: Azure Managed Redis and caching design
flashcards.back: Azure Managed Redis, based on Redis Enterprise, is the in-memory cache and data store to design with, in the Memory Optimized, Balanced, Compute Optimized, and Flash Optimized tiers. Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard, and Premium instances retire on September 30, 2028, and the Enterprise and Enterprise Flash tiers on March 31, 2027. Applications usually use the cache-aside pattern, and Azure Front Door, a CDN, and API Management add other caching layers.
flashcards.detail: A cache is not a system of record. Design for the application to rebuild entries from the database when the cache is empty.

flashcards.back: Build and release pipelines use GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines, signing in to Azure with workload identity federation (OpenID Connect) instead of stored secrets. Infrastructure is declared in Bicep, ARM templates, or Terraform, and rolled out with deployment slots, Container Apps revisions, or Kubernetes GitOps for blue-green or canary releases. Azure Deployment Environments retires on 22 February 2027, so it is not a basis for new designs.
flashcards.detail: A pipeline that authenticates with a long-lived secret is the weak point in a design; a federated credential or managed identity is the fix.

flashcards.back: Azure Migrate is the central hub for discovering servers, databases, and web apps, assessing readiness, right-sizing, and estimating cost, building a business case, analyzing dependencies, and then migrating, using agentless replication for VMware and Hyper-V or an agent-based option for physical servers and other clouds. It integrates with partner tools and with the Database Migration Service.
flashcards.detail: The assessment results decide which of the migration strategies fits each workload, so assessment comes before any migration tool.

flashcards.front: Choosing the SQL Server migration target and method
flashcards.back: SQL Database suits applications that can run without instance-level features. SQL Managed Instance fits near-complete compatibility with SQL Agent and cross-database queries, and can be reached with native backup and restore, the Log Replay Service, or the Managed Instance link for minimal downtime. SQL Server on an Azure VM suits OS-level access or unsupported features. The Database Migration Service runs offline or online migrations to the managed targets.
flashcards.detail: An assessment first shows which features block the move. Online migration is the answer when the business can tolerate only a short cutover window.

flashcards.front: Migrating unstructured data: Data Box, Storage Mover, AzCopy
flashcards.back: Azure Storage Mover is the managed online service for moving files from on-premises or AWS S3 to Azure Storage, with minimal downtime and repeatable jobs. Data Box ships rugged appliances for offline transfer and is suited to data larger than about 40 TB with little or no network capacity; Data Box Disk ships one to five 8-TB SSDs, and Data Box Heavy has been retired. AzCopy is the command-line tool for scripted copies.
flashcards.detail: Enough bandwidth and an online cutover favor Storage Mover or AzCopy. Tens of terabytes over a slow link favor Data Box.

flashcards.back: DDoS IP Protection applies per public IP address and DDoS Network Protection applies to a virtual network and the public IPs in it. Network Protection adds DDoS rapid response support, cost protection for scale-out charges during an attack, discounts on Web Application Firewall, and coverage for Basic-tier public IPs. Both tiers use adaptive tuning against the application's traffic profile and integrate with Azure Monitor and Microsoft Sentinel.
flashcards.detail: A few public IPs without extra services lean to IP Protection. Many IPs in a network, or a need for rapid response and cost protection, lean to Network Protection.

flashcards.back: A managed service that exchanges routes between network virtual appliances and the Azure network using BGP, so routes are learned and updated dynamically instead of maintaining user-defined routes by hand. It simplifies dynamic routing with SD-WAN and firewall appliances and enables transit between ExpressRoute and VPN gateways.
flashcards.detail: A requirement for NVAs to advertise routes without hand-edited route tables points to Route Server.

flashcards.back: A network security perimeter creates a logical boundary around PaaS resources that sit outside your virtual networks, such as Storage accounts, Key Vault, and SQL Database, to control their public network access. Resources are added to a perimeter in Transition (learning, with logging) or Enforced mode, and inbound and outbound rules define what may cross the boundary.
flashcards.detail: Private endpoints bring a PaaS service into a virtual network. A perimeter governs the public path of PaaS-to-PaaS and internet traffic.

flashcards.back: A central management service for virtual networks at scale: network groups collect virtual networks, connectivity configurations build hub-and-spoke or mesh topologies without peering each pair by hand, and security admin rules apply organization-wide rules that are evaluated before network security group rules.
flashcards.detail: A central team that must enforce a rule that application teams cannot override with their own NSGs points to security admin rules.

flashcards.back: Accelerated networking lets a VM's network traffic bypass the host's virtual switch for lower latency and jitter and less CPU use. Proximity placement groups keep related VMs physically close. ExpressRoute FastPath sends data traffic directly to VMs, bypassing the gateway. Front Door and CDN reduce latency to users, and a hub can be placed in the region closest to most traffic.
flashcards.detail: Latency between tiers in one region points to accelerated networking and proximity placement groups. Latency to far-away users points to Front Door or a CDN.

flashcards.front: Azure Front Door Standard vs. Premium
flashcards.back: Both tiers provide global layer-7 routing, caching, TLS offload, and a Web Application Firewall. Premium adds Private Link connections to origins, so that backends such as an internal load balancer or App Service can stay off the public internet, and adds the Microsoft-managed rule set and bot protection that are limited on Standard.
flashcards.detail: A requirement that origins accept traffic only from Front Door over a private connection points to Premium.

questions.question: Fabrikam's security policy forbids storing passwords, or hashes of passwords, in the cloud, and the team will not build federation infrastructure. Sign-in to Entra ID applications must keep working if any single on-premises server fails. Which design meets these requirements?
options: Pass-through authentication, with agents installed on multiple domain-joined hosts
AD FS federation, with two federation servers behind a load balancer
Password hash synchronization, with a second Entra Connect server in staging mode
Pass-through authentication, with one agent on the Microsoft Entra Connect server
questions.explanation: Pass-through authentication validates each password against on-premises AD, so no password or hash is stored in the cloud and no federation farm is needed. Because sign-in fails when no agent is reachable, installing agents on more than one host removes the single point of failure. A single agent meets the password rule but fails the "any single server" requirement. Password hash synchronization stores a hash of the on-premises password hash in Entra ID, which the policy forbids, and a staging-mode server does not change that. AD FS keeps passwords on premises but is exactly the federation infrastructure the team refuses to build.

questions.question: Contoso's 25 administrators permanently hold Global Administrator or subscription Owner. Auditors want privileged access to be time-limited, justified, and approved, with MFA required at the moment of use. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Replace the roles with narrower custom roles at management group scope
Convert the permanent assignments to eligible assignments in PIM
Enable a sign-in risk policy for administrator accounts
Require approval, justification, and MFA in the PIM role settings
Run a monthly access review of the permanent assignments
questions.explanation: Eligible assignments remove standing access, and the PIM role settings enforce approval, justification, and MFA at activation with a bounded duration; together they meet every audit requirement. A monthly access review only recertifies standing assignments, so the access stays standing between reviews. Narrower custom roles change what is permitted, not when or for how long. A sign-in risk policy reacts to suspicious sign-ins and neither time-limits nor approves privileged elevation.

questions.question: A policy assigned at a management group must make sure every storage account has a diagnostic setting that sends logs to a central workspace. Teams create accounts constantly, creation must never be blocked, and a diagnostic setting is a separate resource from the storage account. Which effect should the policy use?
options: DeployIfNotExists
Modify
Append
AuditIfNotExists
questions.explanation: DeployIfNotExists looks for a related resource, here the diagnostic setting, and deploys it when it is missing, without blocking creation of the storage account. AuditIfNotExists performs the same related-resource check but only reports noncompliance; nothing gets deployed. Modify and Append change properties or tags on the resource being evaluated and cannot create a separate resource. Accounts that were already noncompliant before the assignment are corrected by running a remediation task.

questions.question: A conglomerate has three subsidiaries, each with several subscriptions and its own IT team managing its own policies and RBAC. The parent company must enforce one mandatory tagging policy on every subscription, assigned once, and subsidiary teams must not be able to remove it. Which structure should you recommend?
options: A separate Entra tenant per subsidiary, with the tagging policy assigned in each tenant
A parent management group with a child group per subsidiary, assigning the tagging policy at the parent
All subscriptions directly under the tenant root group, with the tagging policy assigned to each subscription
A management group per subsidiary, with the tagging policy assigned separately to each one
questions.explanation: A policy assigned at the parent management group is created once, inherited by every child group and subscription, and cannot be removed by subsidiary administrators who have no rights at the parent scope, while each child group still holds that subsidiary's own policies and RBAC. Assigning the policy separately per child group repeats the work and leaves each subsidiary's owners able to delete their own copy. Subscriptions directly under the root also need one assignment each and give no subsidiary-level grouping. Separate tenants multiply identity administration, and a policy assignment cannot span tenants.
questions.whyTested: Management-group inheritance is the mechanism that delivers 'enforced once from above, independent below'. Each wrong answer sounds organized but repeats the assignment, loses the subsidiary grouping, or fragments the tenant, so the exam is checking whether you pick the structure that actually inherits rather than the one that merely looks tidy.

questions.question: A healthcare group monitors everything through one Log Analytics workspace in East US. Its German clinical subsidiary must keep log data inside Germany, control its own access and retention, and still run its own KQL queries and alerts. How should you change the design?
options: Send the subsidiary's logs to a storage account in Germany through a diagnostic setting
Keep the single workspace and restrict the subsidiary's tables with table-level access control
Keep the single workspace and set a longer retention period on the subsidiary's tables
Create a workspace in Germany West Central for the subsidiary and keep the central one for the rest
questions.explanation: A workspace is bound to one region, so only a dedicated workspace in a German region keeps the data in Germany; it carries its own access and retention settings, and the subsidiary can query and alert on it directly. Table-level access control in the shared workspace still stores the data in East US. A longer table retention changes how long data stays, not where it lives. Archiving to a German storage account satisfies residency but gives up the interactive queries and alerts the subsidiary needs.

questions.question: Contractors from partner firms request access themselves to three applications and a SharePoint site for the length of their contract. A manager must approve each request, and the access must be removed on the contract end date without anyone revoking it by hand. Which Entra ID Governance feature fits?
options: A dynamic group whose membership rule checks a contractor attribute
A recurring access review with results applied automatically
An entitlement management access package with an expiration date
PIM eligible assignments with a fixed end date
questions.explanation: An access package bundles the applications and site, supports a request-and-approval workflow, and its assignments expire on their own. A recurring access review can remove access when its results are applied automatically, but it only runs on a schedule and offers no request, approval, or bundling. A dynamic group grants access while an attribute matches, with no approval step and no end date tied to the contract. PIM eligible assignments govern privileged roles, not application and site access for external users.

questions.question: Operations needs an alert within a minute when a VM's CPU stays above 90%. Security needs to join sign-in events, firewall logs, and VM events across six months of data. Which pairing of Azure Monitor capabilities fits?
options: An activity log alert for CPU; the Activity log for the joins
A metric alert rule on the CPU metric; KQL queries over a Log Analytics workspace
A metric alert for CPU; Metrics Explorer with dimension splitting for the joins
A log search alert on the Perf table for CPU; Metrics Explorer for the joins
questions.explanation: Platform metrics are lightweight numeric time series evaluated every minute, so a metric alert is the fast, cheap way to catch a CPU threshold, while joining several record types across months is exactly what Log Analytics and KQL do. A log search alert can watch CPU but adds ingestion and query latency, and Metrics Explorer cannot join record types. The Activity log records control-plane operations, not performance or security events. Splitting a metric by dimension is not a join, and platform metrics are kept for a limited period.

questions.question: Contoso is building its first enterprise Azure environment. Every new application subscription must start with the same management group placement, policies, RBAC, and a connection to a shared hub network, with no setup work by the application teams. Which approach should you recommend?
options: One shared subscription with a resource group per team and Azure Policy assigned to each group
A Bicep template that each application team runs to deploy a spoke VNet peered to the hub network
An Azure landing zone, with a platform connectivity subscription and new subscriptions created under governed management groups
A management group hierarchy with a policy initiative and RBAC roles assigned at the top level
questions.explanation: A landing zone packages all the pieces: a management group hierarchy carrying inherited policy and RBAC, platform subscriptions hosting the hub network and identity, and a repeatable way to place each new subscription into that structure so it starts governed and connected. A management group hierarchy with policy and RBAC covers governance but delivers no hub connectivity. A template that application teams run themselves covers networking only, depends on each team running it, and brings no governance inheritance. A shared subscription with per-team resource groups blurs billing and scale boundaries and has no new subscriptions to inherit anything.

questions.question: A financial firm is migrating an on-premises SQL Server instance with 12 databases that rely on SQL Agent jobs and cross-database queries. It wants Microsoft to own OS and engine patching and backups, and it will not rewrite the application. Which service should you recommend?
options: Azure SQL Managed Instance
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale
Azure SQL Database elastic pool
SQL Server on an Azure VM with automated patching
questions.explanation: Managed Instance offers near-complete SQL Server engine compatibility, including SQL Agent and cross-database queries, as fully managed PaaS where Microsoft handles OS patching, engine patching, and backups. An elastic pool shares resources among single databases that cannot run SQL Agent jobs or query across databases the way an instance can, and Hyperscale is a single-database service tier with the same limits. SQL Server on a VM with automated patching keeps the features, but the VM, its OS configuration, and its backups remain the customer's responsibility.

questions.question: A messaging app uses a Cosmos DB account with multi-region writes. A user must always see their own just-posted messages after reloading, reads of other users' messages may lag, and the team wants the lowest latency and RU cost that still gives that guarantee. Which consistency level fits?
options: Session
Bounded staleness
Strong
Eventual
questions.explanation: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes and monotonic reads within a client session while staying low-latency and cheap, which is exactly the stated need. Eventual is cheaper still but can return a stale view that omits a user's own post. Bounded staleness limits how stale reads can be for all clients, a stronger and costlier guarantee than needed. Strong is not supported on accounts with multiple write regions, and even where it is available it costs the most latency and RUs.

questions.question: A Cosmos DB container stores IoT telemetry partitioned by deviceType, but 95% of devices share one type. Writes to that logical partition are throttled although most of the container's total RU/s goes unused. Dashboards almost always query one device's readings. What should you do?
options: Raise the container's maximum autoscale RU/s so each partition receives more throughput
Migrate the data to a container partitioned by the device identifier
Migrate the data to a container partitioned by deviceType combined with the datacenter region
Migrate the data to a container partitioned by the ingestion timestamp
questions.explanation: A partition key should have many distinct values and match the common query filter; the device identifier has high cardinality and lines up with per-device queries. A timestamp key is high-cardinality but monotonic, so every current write lands on the newest partition, which creates a different hot spot and scatters per-device queries across partitions. Combining deviceType with a region still yields only a handful of values, so the hot partition remains. More RU/s is divided among physical partitions, so the hot partition still hits its own per-partition limit.

questions.question: A storage account must keep accepting writes without any failover if one datacenter in the primary region is lost. During a regional outage, a reporting app must be able to read the data from a second region without anyone initiating a failover. Which redundancy option should you select?
options: Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) without read access
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) in the primary region
Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS)
Read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS)
questions.explanation: RA-GZRS keeps synchronous copies across three zones in the primary region, so losing a datacenter does not interrupt writes, and replicates asynchronously to a secondary region whose copy is readable at any time. RA-GRS keeps its primary-region copies in one datacenter, so losing it would interrupt writes until a failover. GZRS has the same zone resilience, but its secondary copy cannot be read until a failover occurs. ZRS has no secondary region at all.

questions.question: A legal team keeps seven years of contract records in Blob storage. Each record is opened once or twice a year, and when an attorney asks for one it must open immediately, with no restore step. Storage cost should be as low as possible within that constraint. Which access tier should you use?
options: Cold
Archive
Cool
Hot
questions.explanation: Cold is the lowest-cost tier that is still online, so blobs open immediately, and its higher read cost and 90-day minimum suit records opened once or twice a year. Archive is cheaper to store, but blobs must be rehydrated before they can be read, which can take hours and rules out immediate access. Cool is also online, but it costs more to store than Cold and is aimed at data accessed somewhat more often. Hot has the highest storage cost and is meant for frequently accessed data.

questions.question: A data engineering team runs Spark jobs over petabytes of semi-structured files. Each team needs ACLs at the directory and file level, and nightly jobs rename large folders, which must complete as a single atomic operation. Cost should stay low. Which storage solution fits?
options: Azure Files Premium with an NFS share mounted on each Spark node
Azure NetApp Files with a large capacity pool and snapshots
Blob storage with a flat namespace and RBAC assigned per container
Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (a storage account with hierarchical namespace)
questions.explanation: ADLS Gen2 is Blob storage with a hierarchical namespace, which provides POSIX-style ACLs on directories and files and atomic directory renames at lake scale, at Blob pricing. A flat namespace has no real directories, so renaming a folder means copying and deleting every blob, and RBAC applies at container scope or above rather than per file. Premium Azure Files and Azure NetApp Files are higher-cost file-share services, not lake-scale analytics storage with ACLs.

questions.question: A team plans to move an on-premises SQL Server with 12 databases to Azure SQL Managed Instance, with minimal downtime at cutover. Which step should the team take FIRST?
options: Take full backups of every database and restore them to the target with native restore
Assess the source databases for compatibility blockers, for example with Azure Migrate
Provision a Managed Instance sized to match the source server's CPU and memory
Start an online migration in Database Migration Service and fix errors as they appear
questions.explanation: Assessment comes first because its findings decide whether Managed Instance is a viable target and how to size it; starting a migration before that risks discovering blockers in the middle of a cutover. Starting an online migration in DMS or restoring native backups are migration steps that follow once the target is validated. Provisioning a target to match source hardware guesses at size before real utilization and compatibility data exist.

questions.question: A three-tier VM application must be running in the paired region within one hour of a regional outage, losing no more than 15 minutes of data, with the tiers starting in the correct order. Which service should the design use?
options: Azure Backup with cross-region restore on a GRS vault
Disk snapshots copied to the paired region by a scheduled script
VMs spread across availability zones in the primary region
Azure Site Recovery replication with an ordered recovery plan
questions.explanation: Site Recovery continuously replicates the VMs to the paired region, giving an RPO of minutes, and a recovery plan starts the tiers in order, which meets both targets. Azure Backup with cross-region restore can restore into the paired region, but the RPO is the backup interval and restoring every VM takes far longer than failing over. Availability zones protect against datacenter loss, not a regional outage. Script-copied snapshots have no tier ordering or failover orchestration, and their RPO depends on the script schedule.

questions.question: A line-of-business VM application must stay online if a single datacenter in its region fails, and must be recoverable in another region, with up to 15 minutes of data loss, if the whole region is lost. Which design meets both requirements?
options: VMs in an availability set, replicated to a secondary region with Azure Site Recovery
VMs spread across availability zones, replicated to a secondary region with Azure Site Recovery
VMs spread across availability zones, backed up daily with Azure Backup to a GRS vault
VMs in one availability zone, replicated to a different zone in the same region with Azure Site Recovery
questions.explanation: Spreading the VMs across availability zones keeps the tier running when one datacenter fails, and Site Recovery replicates continuously to another region, giving an RPO of minutes if the whole region is lost. An availability set stays inside one datacenter, so losing that datacenter takes the tier down. A daily backup allows up to a day of data loss, far beyond 15 minutes. Zone-to-zone replication keeps the data in the same region, so a regional loss still takes everything down.

questions.question: An app uses 40 databases on one Azure SQL logical server and a fixed connection string. After a regional outage, all 40 databases must fail over together to a secondary region with no application change. What should you configure?
options: An auto-failover group, with the read-write listener endpoint in the connection string
Geo-restore of each database from geo-redundant backups into the secondary region
Zone-redundant configuration for each database in the primary region
Active geo-replication on each database, failing over each one individually
questions.explanation: An auto-failover group fails every database in the group over together and keeps the read-write listener endpoint stable, so the fixed connection string keeps working. Active geo-replication fails over per database, and each failover changes which server is primary, so connection strings would have to change or be managed database by database. Geo-restore rebuilds each database from backups on a different server, which takes much longer and also changes the server name. Zone redundancy only protects against a datacenter loss inside the primary region.

questions.question: A reporting application must be running again within 4 hours of a regional outage and lose no more than 15 minutes of data. The business wants the lowest cost that meets both targets. Which design should you choose?
options: Keep a hot standby copy of every VM running continuously in the secondary region, with manual failover
Replicate the VMs to the secondary region with Site Recovery, leaving recovery compute unprovisioned until a failover
Back up the VMs hourly to a GRS vault and restore them in the secondary region after an outage
Run the full application in both regions behind Front Door, with a globally replicated database
questions.explanation: Site Recovery replicates continuously, giving an RPO of minutes, and bills only for replication and storage until a failover starts the VMs; recovery within a few hours satisfies a 4-hour RTO, so this is the cheapest design that hits both numbers. Running everything in both regions is the fastest but by far the most expensive, and the RTO does not need it. Hourly backups meet the RTO but can lose up to an hour of data, missing the 15-minute RPO. A hot standby meets both targets but pays for full compute in the second region around the clock, which the cost requirement rules out.
questions.whyTested: This question shape pairs numeric RTO and RPO targets with a cost constraint, so several designs technically work and the skill being tested is picking the cheapest one that still satisfies both numbers, rather than the most resilient-sounding option or the one that merely mentions replication or backup.

questions.question: A global app must keep serving users with no failover delay when a region fails, and users must be able to write data in their nearest region. Which design meets both requirements?
options: Traffic Manager weighted routing to two regions, with an Azure SQL read replica in the second region
Front Door with priority routing to a standby region, with an Azure SQL auto-failover group
Front Door routing to two active regions, with a GRS-replicated storage account as the data tier
Front Door routing to two active regions, with a Cosmos DB account that has multi-region writes
questions.explanation: Front Door can send traffic to two active regions at once, and Cosmos DB with multi-region writes accepts writes in each region, so a regional failure simply removes one active region and no failover step is needed. Priority routing to a standby region with a failover group is active-passive, so recovery takes time. A read replica keeps a single writer, so users far from it still write across regions, and Traffic Manager adds DNS-cache delay. A GRS storage account accepts writes only in its primary region, so the data tier is not active-active.

questions.question: A team will run microservices as containers. They must scale on HTTP load and on queue length, including down to zero instances when idle, and they do not want to operate Kubernetes node pools or cluster upgrades. Which compute service fits?
options: Azure Container Instances container groups
Azure Kubernetes Service with the KEDA add-on
Azure Container Apps
Azure App Service with containers and autoscale rules
questions.explanation: Container Apps provides built-in HTTP and event-driven scaling, including scale to zero, with no cluster to manage. AKS with KEDA can scale the same way, but the team would still own node pools, upgrades, and cluster configuration. An App Service plan keeps at least one instance running, so it cannot scale to zero. Container Instances runs container groups with no autoscaler of its own.

questions.question: A queue-triggered job runs briefly a few times a day. The company wants no compute charge while the job is idle and no servers to manage. Which hosting option fits?
options: An App Service plan with Always On enabled
Azure Container Apps with a minimum of one replica
Azure Functions on a Premium plan with one pre-warmed instance
Azure Functions on a Consumption plan
questions.explanation: A Consumption plan bills per execution and scales to zero, so an idle job costs nothing. A Premium plan keeps at least one pre-warmed instance running and bills for it continuously. A Container Apps app with a minimum of one replica also pays for that replica while idle. An App Service plan is billed for its reserved instances whether or not any code runs.

questions.question: A dozen application teams each own a VNet in one region. All must reach a shared firewall, VPN gateway, and DNS service, but must not reach each other's VNets, and the team wants that isolation without adding custom routing. Which topology fits?
options: Full-mesh peering between all application VNets and the hub
Hub-and-spoke, with each application VNet peered only to the hub VNet
Virtual WAN, with every VNet connected to the hub's default route table
One shared VNet with a subnet and network security group per team
questions.explanation: Peering is non-transitive, so spokes peered only to the hub reach the shared services but cannot reach one another by default; no routing work is needed for isolation. In Virtual WAN, VNets connected to a hub's default route table can reach each other, so isolation would need custom route tables. Full-mesh peering creates direct spoke-to-spoke paths. A single shared VNet abandons the separate VNets each team owns and relies on NSG rules for isolation.

questions.question: A trading firm needs private, predictable-latency connectivity from its datacenter to Azure. The connection must survive an ExpressRoute path failure, the firm wants the lowest added cost, and a few minutes of higher latency during a failure are acceptable. What should you recommend?
options: A second ExpressRoute circuit at a different peering location
ExpressRoute Global Reach linking the datacenter to a second on-premises site
An active-active VPN gateway with two Site-to-Site tunnels over separate internet links
ExpressRoute as the primary path, with a Site-to-Site VPN configured as the failover path
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute provides the predictable private path, and a Site-to-Site VPN can coexist with it as a lower-cost backup that takes over if the circuit fails; the extra latency during a failover is acceptable here. A second circuit at another peering location is the most resilient design but adds the cost of a whole circuit, which the firm wants to avoid. Two VPN tunnels are resilient but give up the predictability of a private circuit entirely. Global Reach links on-premises sites to each other through the Microsoft backbone and does not add a backup path into Azure.

questions.question: A global retailer needs one entry point that sends users to the nearest healthy regional deployment, fails over in seconds rather than waiting on DNS caches, caches static content at the edge, and applies a single WAF policy to all regions. Which should you use?
options: Azure CDN in front of a Standard Load Balancer in each region
Azure Front Door with a global WAF policy
Azure Traffic Manager with an Application Gateway WAF in each region
A single regional Application Gateway v2 with autoscale and WAF
questions.explanation: Front Door is a global layer-7 entry point: it routes by latency and health at the edge with real data-plane failover, caches content at the edge, and enforces one WAF policy centrally. Traffic Manager only answers DNS queries, so failover is bounded by DNS TTL and client caching, and the WAF would have to be configured in every region. A single Application Gateway is regional. A CDN caches content but has no application-aware routing or WAF of its own, and a Standard Load Balancer works at layer 4 within one region.
questions.whyTested: Front Door, Traffic Manager, Application Gateway, and CDN-plus-load-balancer combinations get stacked together constantly because each solves part of the problem at a different layer and scope. This question tests whether you notice the requirement that only a global layer-7 data-path service meets: failover that does not depend on DNS caching, a single central WAF, and edge caching in one service.

questions.question: A hub-and-spoke network must limit workloads' outbound internet traffic to a list of approved domain names, some with wildcards, and log every allowed and denied connection centrally, without maintaining rules on each subnet. Which resource should you deploy in the hub?
options: A NAT gateway on each spoke subnet
Azure Firewall with application rules in a firewall policy
An Application Gateway with WAF in the hub
Network security groups on each spoke subnet that use service tags
questions.explanation: Azure Firewall application rules filter outbound traffic by FQDN, including wildcards, and its logs are centralized, all managed once in the hub. NSGs filter on IP address, port, and protocol, and service tags only name Microsoft-managed address ranges, so they cannot express arbitrary approved domains and would have to be maintained on every subnet. A NAT gateway provides outbound addresses and does no filtering. An Application Gateway with WAF protects inbound web traffic to your apps, not outbound traffic from workloads.

questions.question: Before migrating 400 on-premises VMs, a team must discover them, map which servers communicate with each other so they can be moved in dependent groups, and get right-sized Azure VM recommendations from actual utilization. Which should anchor this phase?
options: Azure Migrate: Server Migration, replicating the VMs to Azure
Azure Migrate discovery and assessment with dependency analysis
Azure Advisor recommendations for the subscription the VMs will land in
The Azure TCO Calculator, using server counts and sizes entered by hand
questions.explanation: Azure Migrate's discovery and assessment collects configuration and performance data from the on-premises VMs, recommends right-sized Azure VMs and costs, and its dependency analysis shows server-to-server connections so related servers move together. The TCO Calculator works from numbers someone types in, so it discovers nothing and cannot see utilization or dependencies. Server Migration is the replication and cutover tool used after assessment. Advisor analyzes resources that are already running in Azure.

questions.question: An order system must process each customer's orders strictly in the sequence submitted, discard duplicate submissions, and set poison messages aside for review. Which service should it use?
options: Azure Event Hubs with the customer ID as the partition key
Azure Event Grid with an event subscription per customer
An Azure Service Bus queue with sessions enabled
Azure Storage queues with a visibility timeout
questions.explanation: Service Bus sessions give first-in-first-out processing per customer, duplicate detection discards repeats, and the dead-letter queue sets poison messages aside. Storage queues offer no FIFO guarantee or built-in duplicate detection. Event Hubs keeps order within a partition, but it is a streaming ingestion service with no dead-lettering or duplicate detection. Event Grid pushes discrete event notifications and does not provide ordered queue processing.

questions.question: A company exposes backend APIs hosted on VMs, App Service, and AKS to external partners. Each partner needs its own subscription key and rate limit, and some responses must be transformed from XML to JSON. Which service should sit in front of the backends?
options: Azure Front Door with a rules engine
Azure Logic Apps with an HTTP trigger
Azure Application Gateway with path-based routing rules
Azure API Management with products and policies
questions.explanation: API Management fronts any backend with per-consumer subscriptions and keys, rate limits and quotas, and policies that transform requests and responses, plus versioning and a developer portal. Application Gateway and Front Door can route by path to different backends, but they do not issue per-partner keys, enforce per-consumer quotas, or transform payloads as an API product. Logic Apps can be made to behave like an API, but it is a workflow engine, not an API gateway.

questions.question: An integration team must connect a SaaS CRM, an on-premises ERP through a data gateway, and SharePoint. Designers want a visual designer with prebuilt connectors, and the flows must be deployed from source control through Bicep pipelines, run under Azure RBAC, and be monitored in Azure Monitor. Which service fits?
options: Azure Functions with Durable Functions
Power Automate cloud flows
Azure Data Factory pipelines
Azure Logic Apps
questions.explanation: Logic Apps provides a visual designer and hundreds of prebuilt connectors as an Azure resource, so workflows deploy with Bicep or ARM, are governed by Azure RBAC, and emit telemetry to Azure Monitor. Power Automate targets business users inside the Power Platform, with a different governance and deployment model. Functions with Durable Functions can orchestrate the same logic but are code-first, with no designer or prebuilt connector catalog. Data Factory moves and transforms data on schedules rather than orchestrating event-driven business workflows.

questions.question: A tenant uses pass-through authentication and also turns on password hash synchronization. If every pass-through authentication agent goes offline, Entra ID does not automatically start validating sign-ins with the synchronized hashes.
questions.explanation: Password hash synchronization enabled alongside pass-through authentication is not an automatic fallback; an administrator would have to switch the sign-in method. Resilience therefore comes from running several authentication agents, since a single agent is a single point of failure, not from having hash sync switched on. A tenant that needs sign-in to survive an on-premises outage with no intervention chooses password hash synchronization as its sign-in method.

questions.question: A Conditional Access policy can be applied when an administrator activates a PIM-eligible role, so activation can demand a stricter control, such as a compliant device, than an ordinary sign-in does.
questions.explanation: PIM role settings can require a Conditional Access authentication context at activation, so a policy bound to that context, for example one requiring a compliant device, is evaluated when the role is activated. PIM controls when privilege is granted and Conditional Access controls the conditions of access, so they are layered rather than substitutes for each other.

questions.question: A user holds Contributor at subscription scope. Assigning that user the Reader role on one resource group makes the user read-only in that resource group.
questions.explanation: Azure RBAC is additive: role assignments combine, and a narrower-scope assignment never removes permissions inherited from a broader scope, so the user stays a Contributor in that resource group. To make the group read-only for that user, narrow the broad assignment instead, for example by assigning Contributor only on the resource groups where it is needed.

questions.question: In an Azure SQL auto-failover group, all databases in the group fail over together as a unit; one database cannot be failed over while the others stay on the original primary server.
questions.explanation: The failover group is the unit of failover: the listener endpoints move for every member database at once, which is what keeps a single connection string valid for the whole application. Failing over one database independently is something active geo-replication does outside a failover group.

questions.question: With Session consistency in Cosmos DB, a user in one client session is guaranteed to immediately read a write that another user committed through a different client session.
questions.explanation: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes and monotonic reads only within a single client session. A different session can see older data for a short time. Only Strong consistency guarantees that every client reads the latest committed write.

questions.question: A storage account's default access tier can be set to Archive, so every new blob lands in the Archive tier automatically.
questions.explanation: Archive is not available as an account-level default. It is assigned per blob after upload, either manually or by a lifecycle management rule, which is why a design that needs data to age into Archive needs a lifecycle policy rather than a default setting.

questions.question: If a file is deleted inside a VM protected by Azure Site Recovery, the deletion is replicated to the secondary region as well, so Site Recovery replication is not a substitute for backup.
questions.explanation: Site Recovery replicates changes continuously, including deletions and corruption, and its recovery points are short-lived points meant for failover. Restoring an accidentally deleted file, or keeping monthly and yearly restore points, is a job for Azure Backup.

questions.question: Because Azure Site Recovery replicates continuously, it can guarantee an RPO of zero when a VM fails over to the secondary region.
questions.explanation: Replication to another region is asynchronous, so the most recent writes may not have reached the target when the primary fails. Site Recovery typically achieves an RPO of seconds to minutes. A design that truly requires zero data loss needs synchronous replication, which is practical only between nearby locations such as availability zones in one region.

questions.question: When a Traffic Manager endpoint fails its health probes, clients are redirected to a healthy endpoint immediately, regardless of DNS caching.
questions.explanation: Traffic Manager only changes the DNS answers it returns. Clients and resolvers that cached the old answer keep using it until the record's TTL expires, so failover is delayed by the probing interval plus the TTL. Front Door sits in the data path and can fail over without waiting on DNS caches.

questions.question: A Virtual WAN hub inspects and filters traffic between connected VNets on its own, so Azure Firewall is not needed to enforce filtering rules between them.
questions.explanation: A virtual hub is a managed routing and connectivity construct; it does not filter traffic by itself. To inspect and filter traffic through the hub, Azure Firewall or a supported third-party security solution is deployed into it, making it a secured virtual hub, and routing configuration steers traffic through that firewall.

questions.question: Which two statements about Privileged Identity Management (PIM) are true? (Choose two.)
options: The scope of an activation is chosen by the user at activation time, regardless of the scope of the eligibility
An activated eligible assignment ends automatically when the configured activation duration elapses
It manages eligible assignments for Azure resource roles, such as Owner on a subscription, as well as Entra directory roles
Approval workflows are available for Entra directory roles but not for Azure resource roles
A user must pass an access review before each activation of an eligible role
questions.explanation: PIM covers both directory roles and Azure resource roles, and every activation is time-bound: it expires when the configured duration ends. Approval can be required for both kinds of role. Access reviews are a separate periodic recertification and do not gate each activation, and an activation cannot exceed the scope at which the user was made eligible.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure Policy effects are true? (Choose two.)
options: A remediation task is how resources found noncompliant by a DeployIfNotExists or Modify policy are corrected after the fact
Policy effects are evaluated only when a resource is created, so existing resources are never assessed
After a Deny policy is assigned, resources that already violate it stay in place and show as noncompliant
A Deny policy assigned at a management group deletes noncompliant resources already deployed in its subscriptions
The Audit effect blocks noncompliant creation requests but still allows updates to existing resources
questions.explanation: Deny acts on create and update requests; resources that already exist are assessed by compliance scans, stay in place, and are reported as noncompliant. Resources flagged by DeployIfNotExists or Modify policies are fixed by running a remediation task. Deny never deletes anything, Audit never blocks a request, and compliance scans do evaluate existing resources.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure management groups are true? (Choose two.)
options: Each management group is its own billing boundary and receives a separate invoice
A subscription can have only one parent management group at a time
A management group hierarchy can span more than one Entra tenant
A policy assignment or role assignment at a management group is inherited by the subscriptions beneath it
A subscription can sit under several management groups so that it inherits policy from each of them
questions.explanation: A subscription has exactly one parent at a time, which keeps inheritance unambiguous, and policy and RBAC assignments flow downward from a management group to everything beneath it. A subscription cannot have several parents, a hierarchy lives inside a single tenant, and management groups are a governance scope rather than a billing boundary; invoicing follows billing accounts and profiles.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure Storage redundancy are true? (Choose two.)
options: In GZRS, the secondary region's copy is spread across the availability zones of that region
In GZRS, the secondary-region copy uses locally redundant storage rather than zone-redundant storage
In RA-GRS, the data in the secondary region becomes readable once a failover has been triggered by Microsoft or the customer
GRS keeps primary-region copies in one datacenter, while GZRS spreads them across availability zones
ZRS protects data against the loss of a whole Azure region as well as a single zone
questions.explanation: GZRS is zone-redundant only in the primary region; its secondary-region copy is stored with LRS. GRS keeps its primary copies in a single datacenter, which is the difference GZRS adds. ZRS stays inside one region, so it cannot survive a regional loss, and RA-GRS exists precisely so that the secondary copy can be read before any failover.

questions.question: Which two statements about Cosmos DB partition key design are true? (Choose two.)
options: Cosmos DB spreads a single hot logical partition across physical partitions to share its load
A monotonically increasing key such as a timestamp tends to concentrate current writes on one partition
Choosing a key that appears in most query filters lets queries target a single partition instead of fanning out
The partition key value of an existing item can be updated in place with a replace operation
A key with only a few distinct values is acceptable because partitions rebalance automatically
questions.explanation: Queries that include the partition key are routed to one partition, while those that do not fan out to every partition at higher cost and latency. A timestamp always increases, so all new writes land on the latest partition. An item's partition key value is immutable: changing it means deleting and recreating the item. A logical partition cannot be split across physical partitions, so Cosmos DB cannot relieve a hot logical partition, and automatic rebalancing moves whole logical partitions, not parts of one.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly distinguish Azure Backup from Azure Site Recovery? (Choose two.)
options: Site Recovery can restore an individual file from a protected VM to an earlier point in time
Azure Backup supports long-term retention, such as monthly and yearly restore points, while Site Recovery recovery points are short-lived
Azure Backup can restore a single file from a VM backup without restoring the whole VM
A Recovery Services vault holds either Backup items or Site Recovery items, not both
Azure Backup can run an ordered recovery plan that fails over each tier of an application in turn
questions.explanation: Backup is built for point-in-time restores, including single-file recovery and retention measured in months or years, while Site Recovery keeps short-lived recovery points for failover. Site Recovery does not offer file-level restore, and the ordered recovery plan belongs to Site Recovery, not Backup. A single Recovery Services vault can hold both Backup and Site Recovery items.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly apply RTO and RPO to a design? (Choose two.)
options: RTO measures how much data is lost, while RPO measures how long the application is unavailable
Tightening the RPO automatically shortens the RTO, because both depend on replication frequency
A design that replicates every 15 minutes cannot meet a 5-minute RPO, however quickly it fails over
A design with an RPO of zero can still miss a 10-minute RTO if failover takes an hour
The RPO is determined by how long the failover process takes to complete
questions.explanation: RPO is about how fresh the recovered data is, so a 15-minute replication interval cannot meet a 5-minute RPO whatever the failover speed, and RTO is about how long recovery takes, so zero data loss does not rescue a slow failover. The two objectives are independent, so tightening one does not shorten the other, and the definitions are reversed in the other statements: RPO limits data loss, RTO limits downtime.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly distinguish Azure Front Door from Azure Application Gateway? (Choose two.)
options: Application Gateway can route users to the nearest of several regions with no service in front of it
Application Gateway lives in a dedicated subnet of your VNet; Front Door is a global service outside any VNet
Front Door can terminate TLS at the edge but cannot route requests by URL path
Application Gateway includes edge caching through built-in integration with Azure CDN
Front Door can use origins outside Azure, such as an on-premises or other-cloud endpoint with a public address
questions.explanation: Application Gateway is deployed into a subnet of a customer VNet and serves one region, while Front Door is a global edge service that can front any origin reachable by a public address, inside or outside Azure. Application Gateway cannot steer users between regions by itself, which is why Front Door or Traffic Manager sits in front of regional gateways. Front Door does route by URL path, and edge caching is a Front Door capability, not an Application Gateway one.

questions.question: Which two statements describe workloads that would justify choosing AKS over Azure Container Apps? (Choose two.)
options: The team wants to scale to zero on HTTP traffic and queue length
The team wants to avoid cluster upgrades and node pool management
The workload needs DaemonSets and full control over node pool configuration
The team writes custom Kubernetes operators and needs direct access to the Kubernetes API
The team wants per-request billing with no infrastructure to size
questions.explanation: Direct Kubernetes API access for custom operators, and DaemonSets or node-pool-level control, are things Container Apps deliberately hides, so they point to AKS. Scale to zero on HTTP or queue triggers, avoiding cluster upgrades and node pools, and consumption-style billing are precisely the reasons to prefer Container Apps.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure ExpressRoute are true? (Choose two.)
options: ExpressRoute encrypts traffic end to end by default, so VPN encryption is unnecessary
Microsoft peering is the routing domain used to reach VNet private IP addresses
Traffic on an ExpressRoute circuit is private but not encrypted by default
An ExpressRoute gateway and a VPN gateway must be placed in separate virtual networks
Private peering is the routing domain used to reach VNet resources by their private IP addresses
questions.explanation: A circuit keeps traffic off the public internet, but private is not the same as encrypted: encryption requires something like IPsec over the circuit or MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct. Private peering is the domain that reaches VNet private addresses, whereas Microsoft peering is used for Microsoft online services and the public endpoints of Azure PaaS services. ExpressRoute and VPN gateways can coexist in one VNet, which is how a VPN is configured as a backup.

questions.question: A company has 15 policy definitions covering tagging, allowed resource types, and encryption, using a mix of Deny, Audit, and DeployIfNotExists effects. All 15 must be assigned together to every new subscription and reported on as a single compliance score. What should you use?
options: A policy initiative (policy set definition) containing the 15 definitions, assigned at a management group
One custom definition whose rule combines the conditions of all 15 policies
The 15 definitions assigned separately at a management group so new subscriptions inherit them
A Bicep template that creates the 15 policy assignments on each new subscription
questions.explanation: An initiative bundles the definitions into one assignable unit with shared parameters and rolls compliance up into one view; assigning it at a management group makes new subscriptions inherit it. Separate assignments at the management group would also be inherited, but they remain 15 assignments to manage and report on. A single custom definition cannot merge rules that use different effects and would lose per-policy compliance detail. A template that creates assignments per subscription still produces 15 assignments each time.

questions.question: Contoso federates most users through AD FS and requires MFA through Conditional Access for every administrator. Leadership wants a guaranteed way to regain admin control if a Conditional Access misconfiguration, an MFA outage, or an on-premises failure blocks every normal sign-in. What should you create?
options: Cloud-only Global Administrator accounts excluded from Conditional Access, with strong unique credentials and sign-in alerts
Global Administrator accounts synchronized from on-premises AD, excluded from Conditional Access and closely monitored
An eligible Global Administrator role in PIM for the CIO, activated with MFA when an emergency arises
Guest accounts from the managed service provider's tenant, assigned Global Administrator for emergencies
questions.explanation: Break-glass accounts must not depend on anything that can fail together with normal sign-in: they are cloud-only, so an AD FS or sync failure cannot affect them, excluded from Conditional Access, protected by strong credentials, and monitored so any use triggers an alert. Synchronized accounts still depend on on-premises infrastructure. A PIM-eligible role needs MFA to activate, which may be the very thing that is broken, and leaves no account that can always sign in. Guests from another tenant depend on that tenant and remain subject to Conditional Access.

questions.question: Application logs in Blob storage are read daily for 30 days, rarely until day 90, and never afterward, but must be kept seven years and then deleted. The team wants this handled automatically with the least administrative effort. What should you configure?
options: A lifecycle management policy: Cool at 30 days, Archive at 90 days, delete at seven years
A timer-triggered Azure Function that scans the container daily and re-tiers or deletes blobs by age
A seven-year time-based immutability policy on the container, applied as soon as logs are written
Blob versioning enabled and the account's default access tier set to Cool for all new logs
questions.explanation: A lifecycle management policy moves blobs between tiers and deletes them based on age with no code to run or maintain. A scheduled Function can reproduce that behavior but is custom code to write, monitor, and pay for. An immutability policy blocks modification and deletion; it neither moves data between tiers nor deletes anything when it expires. Versioning and a Cool default tier change where new blobs start, not how they age into Archive or when they are deleted.

questions.question: A broker-dealer must store trade records so that nobody, including subscription Owners, can modify or delete them until a fixed seven-year period ends. Which configuration meets the requirement?
options: A CanNotDelete resource lock on the storage account itself
A time-based retention policy on the container, then locked
A legal hold applied to the container until the period ends
A time-based retention policy on the container, left unlocked
questions.explanation: A locked time-based retention policy provides write-once, read-many storage: nobody can modify or delete the blobs, and the retention cannot be shortened, until it expires, even with Owner rights. An unlocked policy is intended for testing; its settings can be changed or the policy removed. A legal hold blocks modification and deletion but has no fixed period and can be cleared by anyone with permission to do so. A CanNotDelete lock protects the storage account resource, not the blobs inside it, which can still be deleted through the data plane.

questions.question: Contoso backs up production VMs, which must remain restorable if a whole region is lost, and dev/test VMs, which only need protection from disk or rack failures at the lowest cost. How should the Recovery Services vaults be configured?
options: Production vault on GRS; dev/test vault on GRS to keep one standard
Production vault on ZRS; dev/test vault on LRS
Production vault on GRS; dev/test vault on LRS
Both vaults on ZRS, since zone redundancy covers a regional outage
questions.explanation: A vault's redundancy decides what survives: GRS keeps a copy of the backup data in the paired region, which production needs, while LRS is the cheapest option and still covers disk and rack failures, which is all dev/test needs. ZRS survives a zone loss but stays inside one region, so a regional loss still destroys it; zone redundancy does not cover a regional outage. GRS for dev/test would work but pays for geo-replication nobody asked for.

questions.question: An on-premises application connects to Azure over ExpressRoute and must reach an Azure SQL Database privately, with no traffic crossing the public internet, and the server's public endpoint must be disabled. Which networking feature enables this?
options: ExpressRoute Microsoft peering with a route filter that includes Azure SQL
A private endpoint for the SQL server, in a VNet connected to the ExpressRoute circuit
A firewall rule on the SQL server allowing the on-premises public IP range
A service endpoint on the subnet that hosts the ExpressRoute gateway
questions.explanation: A private endpoint gives the SQL server a private IP address in a VNet; on-premises clients reach that address through the circuit's private peering, and the public endpoint can be disabled. A service endpoint only helps traffic that originates in the subnet and still targets the public endpoint. Microsoft peering carries traffic to the service's public endpoint, which this design wants disabled. A firewall rule allowing public addresses still depends on the public endpoint.

questions.question: Backend VMs span all three availability zones, and the application uses a non-HTTP TCP protocol. The load balancer's frontend IP address must stay available if an entire zone fails, with one frontend address for clients. Which configuration meets this?
options: A Basic Load Balancer (a retired SKU) with VMs from all three zones in its backend pool
Three Standard Load Balancers, one per zone, behind Traffic Manager
A Standard Load Balancer with a zonal frontend pinned to zone 1
A Standard Load Balancer with a zone-redundant frontend IP configuration
questions.explanation: A zone-redundant frontend IP is served from all zones at once, so a single address keeps working when a zone fails.
