A zonal frontend lives in one zone, so losing that zone takes the address down even though backends in other zones are healthy. The Basic SKU (now retired) has no zone support. Three load balancers behind Traffic Manager give three addresses and DNS-based failover, which is more complex and slower than the single zone-redundant address the requirement describes.
questions.whyTested: This tests the Standard Load Balancer's zone-redundant versus zonal frontend distinction, plus the Basic SKU's lack of zone support. The exam likes to probe whether you know a specific SKU or configuration detail decides zone resilience, rather than treating all load balancer setups as interchangeable.

questions.question: A diagnostic setting can send a regional resource's logs to a Log Analytics workspace in a different region, but a storage account destination must be in the same region as the resource.
questions.explanation: Workspace destinations are not tied to the monitored resource's region, which is why one central workspace can collect from many regions; storage account and event hub destinations must be co-located with the resource. A single diagnostic setting can also send to several destinations at once.

questions.question: A Recovery Services vault used to back up an Azure VM must be in the same region as the VM, even when the vault's storage redundancy is GRS.
questions.explanation: Azure Backup requires the vault and the protected VM to share a region; GRS keeps a secondary copy of the backup data in the paired region but does not relocate the vault. This is why one central vault cannot back up VMs from several regions, and one vault per region is needed.

questions.question: Two spoke VNets that are each peered only to a hub can exchange traffic if the hub hosts an Azure Firewall and user-defined routes send spoke traffic to it.
questions.explanation: Peering itself is non-transitive, but a firewall or network virtual appliance in the hub can forward traffic between spokes when route tables send it there. This is the standard way to allow controlled, inspected spoke-to-spoke traffic in a hub-and-spoke design, rather than peering the spokes directly.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure Synapse serverless and dedicated SQL pools are true? (Choose two.)
options: A serverless SQL pool bills for provisioned DWUs even during hours when the pool sits idle
A serverless SQL pool is the more economical choice for a heavy workload that runs around the clock
A dedicated SQL pool can be paused to stop compute charges, while its stored data continues to be billed
A serverless SQL pool can query files in the data lake, such as Parquet or CSV, without first loading them into tables
A dedicated SQL pool bills per terabyte of data processed by each query, instead of for provisioned compute
questions.explanation: A dedicated pool's provisioned compute can be paused to stop compute charges while storage is still billed, and a serverless pool queries files in the lake directly with no loading step. The billing claims about serverless and dedicated pools are swapped in the other statements: serverless bills per data processed with nothing provisioned, and dedicated bills for provisioned DWUs. A constant heavy workload generally suits a dedicated pool better, since per-query billing adds up when the pool would otherwise be busy all day.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure Bastion are true? (Choose two.)
options: Bastion must be deployed into a dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet
Each spoke VNet needs its own Bastion host because Bastion cannot work across VNet peering
The target VM needs a public IP address and an NSG rule allowing RDP or SSH from the internet
A Bastion host deployed in a hub VNet can reach VMs in peered spoke VNets
An agent must be installed on each target VM before Bastion can connect
questions.explanation: Bastion works across VNet peering, so one host in the hub serves peered spokes, and it requires a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet. Targets need no public IP, because Bastion connects to their private addresses, and no agent, since the session is brokered through the portal over TLS.

questions.question: This real Azure Architecture Center diagram shows a hub-spoke network topology. Based on the diagram, which services are centralized in the hub virtual network rather than duplicated in every spoke?
options: Azure Monitor and Azure Firewall, while the VPN/ExpressRoute gateway is deployed in each spoke
The VPN/ExpressRoute gateway alone, because each spoke deploys its own Bastion and Firewall
A separate resource subnet of virtual machines in each spoke
Azure Bastion, Azure Firewall, and the VPN/ExpressRoute gateway
questions.explanation: The hub in the diagram holds the shared Azure Bastion, Azure Firewall, and VPN/ExpressRoute gateway once, so every spoke can use them without deploying its own copy. Each spoke instead holds only its own workload VMs in a resource subnet, which is the point of centralizing shared services in the hub in the first place.

questions.question: In the hub-spoke diagram shown, the two nonproduction spoke virtual networks are connected only by a dotted line labeled "peered or directly connected," while every spoke's solid line runs to the hub. What does this indicate about the topology's default behavior?
options: Spokes automatically gain full connectivity to every other spoke the moment they're peered to the hub, since peering is transitive across a shared hub
Spokes are isolated from each other by default; any spoke-to-spoke path has to be configured separately, on top of the hub peering
Only spokes of the same type, production or nonproduction, are able to reach each other, based purely on that shared classification
The dotted line means those two networks require a full mesh of direct peerings before any traffic between them is possible
questions.explanation: VNet peering is non-transitive, so peering each spoke to the hub does not by itself let two spokes reach each other — that's exactly why the diagram draws spoke-to-spoke connectivity as a separate dotted line rather than as part of the solid hub peering. Any direct or routed spoke-to-spoke path has to be added deliberately.

questions.question: This real Azure Architecture Center diagram shows a VM workload deployed into an Azure landing zone, split into an "Azure application landing zone subscription" and an "Azure platform landing zone subscription." According to the diagram, who owns the hub virtual network, Azure Firewall, and Azure Bastion shown in the platform landing zone subscription?
options: The same workload team that owns the application landing zone subscription, so one team controls every subscription
A central platform team, separate from the workload team that owns the application landing zone subscription
A managed service provider that administers both subscriptions on the workload team's behalf
Each application team, which deploys its own copy of the hub, firewall, and Bastion inside its subscription
questions.explanation: The diagram draws a clear line between the application landing zone subscription (workload-owned resources like the Application Gateway and VM scale sets) and the platform landing zone subscription (the hub, Firewall, and Bastion), matching the landing zone principle that a central platform team owns and maintains shared connectivity and security services. Having each application team deploy its own hub, firewall, and Bastion would defeat the purpose of a shared platform subscription, and nothing in the diagram hands either subscription to a single team or an outside provider.

questions.question: In the landing zone diagram shown, the frontend and backend VM scale sets are each spread across Zone 1, Zone 2, and Zone 3, behind a zone-redundant Application Gateway and a zone-redundant internal load balancer. What failure does spreading VMs across three zones like this protect against?
options: A misconfigured network security group rule that blocks traffic
The loss of a single datacenter (availability zone) within the region
Accidental deletion or corruption of data on the VMs' disks
The loss of an entire Azure region, including every availability zone in it
questions.explanation: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within one region, so spreading VMs and the load balancer's frontend across three of them protects against losing any single one of those datacenters. A full regional outage would take out every zone at once and needs a secondary region instead, which this diagram's single-region zone spread does not provide. Zones do nothing about deleted data or a bad NSG rule, which are failures every zone would share.

questions.question: This real Azure Architecture Center decision-tree diagram helps choose an Azure compute service. According to the flowchart, a workload being newly built (not migrated) that can be containerized, needs full-fledged orchestration, and isn't using Azure Red Hat OpenShift is directed to which service?
options: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Azure Functions
Azure Batch
Azure Virtual Machines
questions.explanation: Following that exact path through the flowchart — new build, containerizable, needs full orchestration, not OpenShift — lands on Azure Kubernetes Service. Functions and Batch sit on different branches for event-driven or high-performance-computing workloads, and plain VMs are the answer only when full OS control is required, earlier in the tree.

questions.question: According to the same decision tree, an event-driven workload made up of short-lived processes, being built new rather than migrated, is directed to which service — before the flowchart ever asks about container orchestration?
options: Azure Functions
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Azure VMware Solution
Azure Red Hat OpenShift
questions.explanation: The flowchart routes a new, event-driven, short-lived-process workload straight to Azure Functions, ahead of the branches that ask about containerization or orchestration needs at all — matching Functions' role as event-triggered, per-execution-billed compute for exactly this kind of workload.

questions.question: This real Azure Architecture Center decision-tree diagram for choosing a load-balancing service asks whether traffic is Layer 7 and, if so, whether the deployment spans multiple regions. According to the flowchart, which service is recommended for global, multi-region, Layer-7 (HTTP/HTTPS) traffic when built-in CDN caching is also wanted?
options: Azure Front Door
Azure Load Balancer
Azure Traffic Manager alone, with no other service
Application Gateway alone, without Traffic Manager
questions.explanation: The flowchart's global, Layer-7, CDN-wanted branch points specifically to Azure Front Door, noted on the diagram as recommended for PaaS backends because of its built-in CDN. The Traffic Manager + Application Gateway combination is the flowchart's answer for a different branch — global Layer-7 traffic into a multi-region VNet deployment, without CDN caching.

questions.question: According to the same decision tree, internal (not internet-facing) clients needing a passthrough load balancer that supports TCP and UDP protocols are pointed to which service?
options: Azure Load Balancer
Azure Application Gateway
Azure Front Door
Azure API Management
questions.explanation: The flowchart's "passthrough load balancer" branch for internal clients leads to Azure Load Balancer, labeled on the diagram as supporting TCP and UDP protocols. Application Gateway sits on the neighboring "terminating load balancer" branch for TCP/TLS traffic instead, and Front Door and API Management appear only on the internet-facing branches.

questions.question: This real Azure Architecture Center diagram shows a single table split into an "A-G" shard and an "H-Z" shard, purely based on each row's key. What kind of data partitioning strategy does this illustrate?
options: Vertical partitioning, where columns are divided by how often they are accessed
Horizontal partitioning, where rows are divided by a key range
Functional partitioning, where data is divided by subdomain or bounded context
Replication, where each shard holds a full copy of the table
questions.explanation: Splitting the same rows into separate shards purely by a key range (A-G versus H-Z) is horizontal partitioning, also called sharding: every row keeps the same columns, but each row lives in exactly one shard based on its key. That is different from vertical partitioning (splitting columns), functional partitioning (splitting by subdomain), or replication, where every copy would hold all the rows.

questions.question: In the sharding diagram shown, every row from the original table lands in exactly one of the two shards, split by key range. If real-world traffic turned out to concentrate heavily on keys in the "A-G" range while the "H-Z" shard sat nearly idle, what problem would this illustrate?
options: A hot partition, where an uneven key distribution overloads one shard regardless of how much capacity is provisioned
A consistency-level misconfiguration, where too weak a level lets reads pile up on whichever shard answers fastest
A geo-redundancy failure, where the secondary region silently stops receiving replicated writes for one shard
An access-tier misconfiguration, where one shard was left on a cheaper, lower-throughput storage tier than the other
questions.explanation: Concentrating traffic on one key range like this is exactly what a hot partition looks like — the partitioning scheme, not the amount of provisioned throughput or any consistency or storage setting, is what's causing one shard to take nearly all the load while the other sits idle. The fix is redesigning the partition key, not raising capacity or changing consistency.

questions.question: Contoso wants MFA required only when employees sign in to Microsoft 365 from unmanaged devices outside the corporate network, with legacy authentication blocked for everyone. Which should you configure?
options: Security defaults, with legacy authentication blocked tenant-wide
Per-user MFA set to Enforced for every employee
Conditional Access policies with device and location conditions
A named location that lists the trusted corporate IP ranges
questions.explanation: Conditional Access evaluates signals such as device state and location at sign-in and then applies a control, so it can require MFA only in the risky case and block legacy authentication through a separate policy. Security defaults apply one fixed baseline to everyone and cannot be limited to unmanaged devices outside the network. Per-user MFA is all-or-nothing and cannot consider device or location. A named location is only an input that a Conditional Access policy can use; on its own it enforces nothing.

questions.question: An application writes to a GRS storage account. The team wants a read-only reporting service to read from the secondary region during normal operation, with no other change to how data is replicated. What should they do?
options: Keep GRS and give the reporting service a read-only SAS token for the primary endpoint
Enable read access to convert the account to RA-GRS, and point the reporting service at the account's secondary endpoint
Convert the account to GZRS, whose secondary-region copy is readable by default
Enable read access to convert the account to RA-GRS; the existing primary endpoint then serves reads from either region
questions.explanation: Enabling read access converts GRS to RA-GRS and exposes the replicated copy at a separate secondary endpoint (the account name with a -secondary suffix), so the reporting code must be pointed at it and must tolerate slightly stale data because replication is asynchronous. The primary endpoint never redirects reads to the secondary. GZRS adds zone redundancy in the primary region, but its secondary copy is not readable unless read access (RA-GZRS) is enabled. A read-only SAS token limits permissions on the primary but does not read from the secondary.

questions.question: Production VM backups go to a GRS Recovery Services vault. In an annual DR drill, the team wants to restore VMs from the backups into the paired region on demand, without waiting for Microsoft to declare a regional disaster. What should you do?
options: Switch the vault's storage redundancy to ZRS
Create a second vault in the paired region and register the same VMs with it
Enable Cross Region Restore on the vault
Enable Azure Site Recovery replication for each VM
questions.explanation: Cross Region Restore lets you restore from the secondary-region copy of a GRS vault on demand, including for drills. A vault must be in the same region as the VMs it protects, so a second vault in the paired region cannot back up those VMs. ZRS is a different scope, zones within one region, and gives up the secondary-region copy altogether. Site Recovery replication would add failover capability, but it is not a way to restore from the existing backups, which is what the drill is meant to validate.

questions.question: A workload behind Azure Front Door serves cached static assets and dynamic API calls that must keep reaching the same regional backend for a given user session. How should you configure Front Door so the API calls stay pinned without breaking static caching?
options: Place Traffic Manager with priority routing in front of Front Door to hold each user on one region
Send API paths to an origin group with session affinity on, and static paths to a cached route
Disable caching on every route so each request is evaluated for routing again
Raise the origin group's latency sensitivity so the same origin usually wins each request
questions.explanation: Session affinity is set on the origin group and caching is set per route, so splitting the paths gives each kind of request the behavior it needs. Disabling caching everywhere gives up a working optimization and does not pin sessions anyway. Putting Traffic Manager in front adds a DNS layer that cannot pin a session to one backend behind Front Door. Latency sensitivity only widens which origins count as fastest; it does not guarantee the same origin each time.

questions.question: A company uses PIM for just-in-time elevation. Each quarter, the role owner must document a decision on whether each eligible administrator still needs the role, and those who do not should lose eligibility. What should you add?
options: A Conditional Access policy requiring a compliant device when the role is activated
A quarterly access review of the role's eligible assignments, with decisions applied automatically
A PIM role setting that makes every eligible assignment expire after 90 days
An entitlement management access package for the role, with a 90-day expiration
questions.explanation: An access review has the role owner or another reviewer attest to each assignment, records the decision for auditors, and can remove eligibility automatically. Expiring eligibility removes access on a timer without anyone deciding that it is no longer needed and forces administrators to re-request it. A compliant-device condition changes how activation happens, not whether the eligibility continues. An access package is built for requesting and expiring access to apps, groups, and sites, and does not have the role owner attest to existing eligibility.

questions.question: An administrator deleted a container holding thousands of blobs. Blob soft delete was enabled on the account with a 14-day retention, yet the team cannot restore the container's contents. Which feature should have been enabled to make this recoverable?
options: Container soft delete
A time-based immutability policy on the container
Blob versioning
The change feed
questions.explanation: Blob soft delete protects individual blobs; deleting the whole container bypasses it. Container soft delete retains a deleted container and its blobs for a configurable window so they can be restored. Versioning keeps prior versions of each blob, but those versions are deleted along with the container. The change feed only logs changes and cannot restore anything. An immutability policy would have prevented the blobs from being deleted, but it does not make an already-deleted container recoverable.

questions.question: Azure Bastion is deployed in a hub VNet. Spoke VMs have only private IPs, and each spoke subnet has an NSG that denies other inbound traffic. Administrators cannot connect through Bastion. What should you change?
options: Remove the NSGs from the spoke subnets, because Bastion connections bypass NSG evaluation
Assign a public IP to each VM and restrict it to Bastion's public IP in the NSG
Add an inbound rule to the spoke NSGs allowing RDP and SSH from the AzureBastionSubnet address range
Allow RDP and SSH from the Internet service tag, because Bastion connects from public addresses
questions.explanation: Bastion reaches the VM's private IP from the AzureBastionSubnet, and the VM's NSG still evaluates that traffic, so it needs an inbound allow rule scoped to that subnet's address range. NSGs are not bypassed, and removing them would drop a layer of defense. Bastion's connection to the VM originates from its subnet's private addresses, not the internet, so allowing the Internet tag is both unnecessary and too broad. Giving each VM a public IP defeats the purpose of using Bastion.

questions.question: A payments platform needs an RTO under two minutes and can afford infrastructure in two regions, but its data layer cannot safely accept concurrent writes in two regions without risking double-processed payments. Which topology best fits?
options: A single region with availability zones, accepting the risk of a regional outage
Pilot light: the replicated database runs in the second region, and the app tier starts after a failure
Warm standby: the app tier runs in the second region and its replicated database is promoted on failure
Active-active, with both regions accepting writes behind a global load balancer
questions.explanation: A warm standby keeps the application tier running in the second region and promotes a replicated database on failure, so only one region ever accepts writes, which avoids double-processed payments, and the running app tier lets recovery fit a two-minute RTO. Active-active would reintroduce the concurrent-write conflict the scenario rules out. A pilot light starts the app tier only after a failure, and that start-up time would exceed a two-minute RTO. A single region with zones does not survive a regional outage.

questions.question: Security requires examining the contents of outbound HTTPS traffic from the spokes for malicious payloads and detecting known attack signatures, with the capability managed centrally in the hub. Which should you deploy?
options: Azure Firewall Premium with TLS decryption and IDPS
Azure Firewall Standard with threat intelligence filtering
Network security group flow logs with Traffic Analytics
Azure Firewall Basic with application rules
questions.explanation: Only the Premium SKU can decrypt outbound TLS so the contents can be examined, and it adds a signature-based intrusion detection and prevention system (IDPS), both managed centrally in the hub. Standard filters on FQDNs, network rules, and threat intelligence but cannot look inside encrypted payloads. NSG flow logs (being retired on 30 September 2027 in favor of virtual network flow logs) record who talked to whom and do not inspect content. The Basic SKU is a reduced-feature option intended for small environments.

questions.question: A release pipeline deletes and recreates 12 Function Apps on every deployment. All of them need to read secrets from the same Key Vault, and the team wants to grant that permission once and have it survive every recreation. What should you do?
options: Create one user-assigned managed identity, attach it to all 12 apps, and grant it the Key Vault role once
Enable a system-assigned managed identity on one app and let the other eleven use that identity
Store a service principal secret in each app's settings and grant the principal the Key Vault role once
Enable a system-assigned managed identity on each app and have the pipeline re-grant the Key Vault role after each deployment
questions.explanation: A user-assigned identity is a standalone resource: it can be attached to many apps and keeps its role assignment when the apps are deleted and recreated. A system-assigned identity is created and deleted with its app, so every recreation produces a new principal that needs the role granted again, which the pipeline would have to script. An app cannot borrow another app's system-assigned identity. A shared service principal secret works but brings back secret storage and rotation, which managed identities exist to avoid.

questions.question: A policy must add a missing CostCenter tag, with a default value, to resources as they are created, and must also be able to fix the tag on thousands of existing resources through remediation. Creation must not be blocked, and no separate resource should be deployed. Which effect fits?
options: Audit
DeployIfNotExists
Modify
Append
questions.explanation: Modify adds or updates tags on the resource itself and, through a remediation task, can correct existing resources as well. Append also adds fields during a create or update request, but it only acts on those requests, cannot be remediated against existing resources, and Microsoft recommends Modify for tags. DeployIfNotExists deploys a separate related resource, which is not needed here. Audit only reports noncompliance.

questions.question: A team is moving an existing app built on MongoDB drivers and aggregation queries to a fully managed, globally distributed database. It wants the fewest application code changes and no database servers to operate. Which should you choose?
options: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, rewriting the data access layer to its SDK
MongoDB Community Edition on VMs in two regions with replica sets
Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, storing documents as JSONB
questions.explanation: Cosmos DB for MongoDB speaks the MongoDB wire protocol, so existing drivers and queries work with few changes, and it is a managed service with global distribution. Cosmos DB for NoSQL is the native API and a strong choice for new apps, but it means rewriting data access against a different query model. Storing documents as JSONB in PostgreSQL also needs a rewrite. MongoDB on VMs keeps the code but leaves replication, patching, and failover to the team.

questions.question: A team migrates a PostgreSQL application and needs automatic failover if an entire availability zone fails, with no committed transactions lost. It must keep the PostgreSQL engine and minimize administration. What should you recommend?
options: PostgreSQL on Azure VMs in two zones with streaming replication
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with zone-redundant high availability
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with a read replica in another zone, promoted manually
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with same-zone high availability
questions.explanation: Zone-redundant high availability keeps a standby in another zone with synchronous replication, so committed transactions are not lost and failover is automatic, all managed by the service. Same-zone high availability also fails over automatically, but its standby shares the primary's zone and does not survive a zone failure. A read replica replicates asynchronously, so recent commits can be lost on promotion, and promotion is a manual step. Self-managed VM replication could be built to meet the targets but puts replication, patching, and failover orchestration on the team.

questions.question: A storage account has a private endpoint, and VNet clients resolve its name to the private IP through a linked Private DNS zone. On-premises clients connected over ExpressRoute still resolve the name to the public IP. What should you add?
options: An A record for the storage account name in a public Azure DNS zone, pointing to the private IP
A conditional forwarder on the on-premises DNS servers that targets a DNS resolver in the VNet
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on the gateway subnet so on-premises traffic stays private
A conditional forwarder on the on-premises DNS servers pointing to the address 168.63.129.16
questions.explanation: Private DNS zone records can only be resolved from linked VNets, so on-premises DNS must forward the relevant queries to something in Azure that can answer them, such as an Azure DNS Private Resolver inbound endpoint or a DNS forwarder VM in the VNet. The address 168.63.129.16 is a virtual IP reachable only from inside Azure, so on-premises servers cannot use it. A public DNS zone would publish a private address on the internet, and the storage service's own public domain is not a zone the customer controls. A service endpoint gives on-premises traffic no private path and does nothing for name resolution.

questions.question: A subnet full of backend VMs behind a Standard Load Balancer is making a very high volume of outbound connections to a handful of external API endpoints, and administrators see intermittent failures consistent with SNAT port exhaustion. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Associate a NAT gateway with the subnet to provide dedicated outbound SNAT capacity
Add an inbound NAT rule to the load balancer for each VM
Enable zone redundancy on the load balancer's frontend IP configuration
Lower the idle timeout and enable TCP reset on the load-balancing rules
questions.explanation: A NAT gateway provides a much larger, dedicated pool of outbound SNAT ports for a subnet, directly relieving the exhaustion a Standard Load Balancer's default outbound behavior can hit under heavy connection volume. Lowering the idle timeout and enabling TCP reset releases ports sooner, which can ease the symptom but adds no capacity. Inbound NAT rules affect inbound traffic to specific VMs, not outbound SNAT. Zone redundancy on the frontend addresses availability across zones, not port exhaustion.

questions.question: A two-VM application tier must survive a single-rack power failure and Azure's planned host maintenance without both VMs going offline. The VMs exchange synchronous traffic, so the business wants both to stay in one datacenter. What is the simplest configuration that fits?
options: Place both VMs on a single Azure Dedicated Host for isolation
Place both VMs in a proximity placement group to keep them physically close
Place the VMs in different availability zones of the same region
Place both VMs in an availability set, spread across fault and update domains
questions.explanation: An availability set spreads VMs over fault domains (separate racks with independent power and network) and update domains (staggered maintenance reboots) inside one datacenter. Availability zones would protect against both failures, but they place the VMs in different datacenters, which the business ruled out. A proximity placement group does the opposite of spreading: it packs VMs close together for latency and offers no rack-level resilience. A single dedicated host is one physical machine, so a host failure or maintenance event takes both VMs down.

questions.question: A single-region application depends on a web tier (App Service, 99.95% SLA) and a database (Azure SQL Database, 99.99% SLA), with no redundant paths. The business requires 99.95% availability end to end. What is the composite SLA, and does the design meet the requirement?
options: About 99.94%, which falls just short of the requirement
99.99%, because the database's higher SLA covers gaps in the web tier
About 99.97%, because the two SLAs are averaged
99.95%, because the lowest SLA in the chain sets the composite
questions.explanation: Dependencies in series multiply: 0.9995 x 0.9999 is about 0.99940, or 99.94%, which is below 99.95%. Adding a redundant path, such as a second region behind Front Door, is how a design recovers the gap. Taking the lowest SLA ignores the extra failure risk of the second dependency, a higher SLA never compensates for a weaker one in series, and SLAs are multiplied, not averaged.

questions.question: Break-glass emergency access accounts should be synchronized from on-premises Active Directory, so their passwords follow the same policies as every other administrator account.
questions.explanation: Break-glass accounts should be cloud-only so that an on-premises outage, a sync failure, or a federation problem can never be what locks the organization out. Their protection comes from long, unique credentials stored securely and from monitoring and alerting on any sign-in, not from inheriting on-premises account policies.

questions.question: After a time-based retention policy on a blob container is locked, its retention period can still be extended, but it can no longer be shortened or removed.
questions.explanation: Locking makes the policy irreversible in the weakening direction: the interval can be increased but never decreased, and the policy cannot be removed. Extending is allowed because it only strengthens protection. This one-way behavior is what makes locked mode suitable for regulatory write-once, read-many requirements.

questions.question: An Ultra Disk can be used as the operating system disk of a virtual machine.
questions.explanation: Ultra disks are data disks only; an OS disk uses a Standard SSD, Premium SSD, or Standard HDD managed disk. Ultra Disk is chosen for latency-sensitive data volumes where IOPS and throughput must be tuned independently of capacity.

questions.question: Azure Site Recovery can replicate Azure VMs from one availability zone to another in the same region, not only to a different region.
questions.explanation: Zone-to-zone disaster recovery is supported for Azure VMs in regions that have availability zones. It protects against the loss of a zone while keeping data inside the region, so it does not protect against a regional outage; that still requires replication to a secondary region.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly distinguish Azure RBAC from Azure Policy? (Choose two.)
options: Azure Policy can reject a deployment requested by a user who holds the Owner role on the subscription
A role assigned at a management group and a policy assigned there both apply to every subscription beneath it
Azure Policy decides by checking who the requesting user is, while RBAC checks the properties of the resource
Assigning an Azure Policy to a user gives that user permission to manage the resources in scope
A custom role definition can limit a Contributor to creating resources only in approved regions
questions.explanation: Policy evaluates the properties of what is being deployed and applies to everyone at its scope, including Owners, and both RBAC role assignments and policy assignments inherit downward from a management group. RBAC cannot express a condition such as an allowed region, because a role definition lists operations, not resource properties. A policy never grants permissions to anyone, and the claim that Policy checks the user while RBAC checks resource properties has the two services reversed: RBAC checks who is acting, while Policy checks what is being created.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly distinguish blob soft delete, legal holds, and locked retention policies? (Choose two.)
options: A legal hold ends automatically when the container's retention interval elapses
A legal hold stays in effect until someone explicitly clears it, with no built-in expiry
Soft delete satisfies write-once, read-many requirements because deleted blobs can always be restored
A locked time-based retention policy can be shortened by an Owner after a formal approval process
Soft delete does not stop a user with delete permission from deleting a blob; it only keeps the deleted blob recoverable for a retention window
questions.explanation: Soft delete is recovery-focused: deletion still happens, and the blob is restorable only for the retention window. A legal hold is open-ended; it persists until an authorized user clears it. A locked retention policy cannot be shortened by anyone, including an Owner. Soft delete does not meet write-once, read-many requirements because blobs can still be deleted and eventually expire from the recoverable state, and a legal hold has no connection to a retention interval.

questions.question: Which two statements about Virtual Machine Scale Sets are true? (Choose two.)
options: Autoscale rules can be based on CPU percentage but not on a schedule or on queue length
Autoscale changes how many instances run; it does not resize the VM SKU of existing instances
Spreading a scale set across zones keeps the tier running if the whole region is lost
Autoscale can move instances from Standard SSD to Premium SSD disks when load rises
Instances of one scale set can be spread across multiple availability zones
questions.explanation: Autoscale adds or removes instances, so it is scale out and in, not a change of VM size, and instances can be distributed across zones for zone-level resilience. Zones sit inside one region, so they do not survive a regional outage, autoscale does not change disk types, and rules can be driven by metrics such as queue length as well as by a schedule.

questions.question: Regulations require monthly restore points for seven years but only 30 days of daily restore points. Which two statements about configuring this in Azure Backup are true? (Choose two.)
options: One backup policy can combine 30 days of daily retention with 84 months of monthly retention
Each retention tier needs its own Recovery Services vault so the policies do not conflict
Monthly and yearly restore points are existing scheduled backups that are kept longer, not extra backup jobs
Setting the daily retention to 84 months keeps the same restore points as the monthly rule at lower cost
Site Recovery recovery points can be retained for seven years to cover the monthly requirement
questions.explanation: Daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly retention are configured independently on one policy, and the longer-term points are simply selected scheduled backups that are retained longer, which is how the grandfather-father-son pattern keeps long reach at low cost. Retaining every daily point for 84 months would store far more data than the monthly rule. Site Recovery recovery points are short-lived and not meant for multi-year retention, and retention tiers do not need separate vaults.

questions.question: Which two statements about availability sets are true? (Choose two.)
options: Fault domains group VMs that share power and network hardware, so spreading VMs across them limits hardware-failure impact
An availability set can span several datacenters, so it survives the loss of one datacenter
Update domains group VMs that share a rack, power source, and network switch
During planned maintenance, Azure restarts one update domain at a time
A VM can belong to an availability set and an availability zone at the same time
questions.explanation: Fault domains are the hardware boundary (shared rack, power, and network), and update domains stagger planned-maintenance reboots one group at a time. Update domains are not hardware groupings, so the rack, power, and switch description belongs to fault domains. An availability set lives within a single datacenter, and a VM is placed either in an availability set or in an availability zone, not both.

questions.question: A managed service provider administers Azure subscriptions for 30 customers, each in its own Entra tenant. Engineers must sign in only with the provider's own identities and MFA, customers must keep ownership and be able to revoke access, and the provider wants one view across all subscriptions. What should you use?
options: Cross-tenant synchronization to create member accounts for engineers in each customer tenant
Azure Lighthouse with delegated Azure RBAC roles for the provider's engineer groups
B2B guest accounts for each engineer in each customer tenant, with roles assigned per tenant
Transferring each customer subscription into the provider's tenant under one management group
questions.explanation: Lighthouse lets engineers manage delegated subscriptions from their own tenant with their own identities and MFA, customers keep ownership and can remove the delegation, and the provider sees every customer in one view. B2B guests or synchronized member accounts need separate accounts and sign-in context in each of 30 tenants, and each customer's own policies apply to them. Moving subscriptions into the provider's tenant transfers control to the provider, which is exactly what the customers want to avoid.

questions.question: A CISO wants a continuously updated measure of how well the company's Azure subscriptions follow security benchmark recommendations, such as open management ports and unencrypted storage, with prioritized fixes. The company has no need for a SIEM. Which service should provide it?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud, using its Secure Score
Microsoft Sentinel, with analytics rules on subscription activity
The Azure Policy compliance dashboard for a built-in initiative
Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk detections
questions.explanation: Defender for Cloud assesses resource configuration against security benchmarks, produces prioritized recommendations, and rolls them into a Secure Score tracked over time. Sentinel is a SIEM and SOAR that detects and responds to threats from collected logs, which the scenario says is not needed. The Policy compliance view reports pass or fail against policy rules but does not score or prioritize security posture. Entra ID Protection detects risky identities and sign-ins, not resource configuration.

questions.question: A user assigned Owner on a storage account can read the blob contents when requests are authorized with Microsoft Entra ID, with no additional role assignment.
questions.explanation: Owner and Contributor grant control-plane Actions such as managing the account. Reading blob data through Entra authorization needs data-plane permissions (DataActions), usually through a role such as Storage Blob Data Reader or a custom role that lists DataActions. Control-plane roles can retrieve account keys, which is a separate path that bypasses Entra data authorization, and many designs disable shared-key access for exactly that reason.

questions.question: A transactional Azure SQL Database is expected to grow to 60 TB. Backups must not slow the workload, several read replicas must be addable quickly for reporting, and the app must keep using T-SQL unchanged. Which service tier should you recommend?
options: SQL Managed Instance Business Critical
The DTU model's Premium tier
The vCore model's Business Critical service tier
The vCore model's Hyperscale service tier
questions.explanation: Hyperscale separates compute from storage: it supports databases far larger than the other options, takes backups from storage snapshots that do not burden compute, and scales reads out with replicas quickly. Business Critical, Managed Instance, and DTU Premium all top out well below 60 TB, and their backups and replicas are tied to the compute tier.

questions.question: A new Cosmos DB workload in a single region needs roughly 2,000 RU/s for a few minutes, a few times a week, and is idle the rest of the time. The team wants no charge for provisioned capacity while idle. Which option fits?
options: Autoscale provisioned throughput with a 4,000 RU/s maximum
Serverless capacity mode
Standard provisioned throughput of 2,000 RU/s with reserved capacity
Provisioned throughput lowered and raised by a scheduled Azure Function
questions.explanation: Serverless bills only for the request units consumed, so idle time costs nothing, and this occasional peak fits within its limits. Autoscale never drops below 10% of its maximum, so a 4,000 RU/s maximum still bills at least 400 RU/s every hour. Standard provisioned throughput bills the full 2,000 RU/s around the clock, and a reservation discounts that without removing it. A scheduled function can lower provisioned throughput, but only down to the container's minimum, and it adds a component to maintain.

questions.question: A serverless SQL pool query that scans a large CSV file in the data lake is billed for the data it processes, even if the query returns only a few rows.
questions.explanation: Serverless pricing is based on the amount of data a query processes, not on the size of its result. That is why columnar formats such as Parquet, where a query reads only the columns it needs, can cut cost sharply compared with scanning CSV, and why a constant heavy workload can be cheaper on a dedicated pool.

questions.question: Which two statements about Cosmos DB capacity modes are true? (Choose two.)
options: A serverless account can be configured with multi-region writes
Autoscale provisioned throughput stops billing completely whenever a container is idle
A serverless container has an upper limit on total storage that a provisioned-throughput container does not have
Autoscale provisioned throughput bills for at least 10% of its configured maximum RU/s, even when no requests arrive
Serverless capacity mode is the better choice for sustained heavy traffic that needs predictable performance
questions.explanation: Autoscale scales between 10% of its maximum and the maximum, so an idle container still bills for that floor, and serverless containers have a storage cap that provisioned containers do not. Sustained, heavy, predictable traffic suits provisioned throughput rather than serverless, serverless is not available with multi-region writes, and autoscale never bills zero.

questions.question: A team has already implemented availability zones, a secondary region, and automated failover for a critical workload. It now wants to see how the running production architecture behaves when a dependency becomes slow or a VM is killed, rather than trusting the design on paper. Which service should it use?
options: Azure Chaos Studio
Application Insights availability tests
Azure Site Recovery test failover
Azure Load Testing
questions.explanation: Chaos Studio injects faults, such as killing a VM or adding latency to a dependency, into a running environment so the team can observe how the real architecture responds. Site Recovery test failover validates that replicated VMs are recoverable, not how a live system tolerates faults. Load Testing generates traffic to measure performance under load and does not simulate component failure. Availability tests probe whether an endpoint responds, so they detect an outage but do not cause one to see how the system copes.

questions.question: A Cosmos DB account has multi-region writes enabled in East US, West Europe, and Southeast Asia. East US becomes unavailable. What happens to write traffic?
options: A failover priority list promotes one remaining region to be the sole write region after a delay
Writes stop until an administrator manually starts a failover
Writes continue in the other two regions, and the SDK redirects the app using its preferred regions list
The remaining regions become read-only until East US recovers, to avoid write conflicts
questions.explanation: With multi-region writes every region already accepts writes, so no promotion is needed: the remaining regions keep serving writes, and the SDK sends requests to the next region in the app's preferred regions list. A failover priority list matters for accounts with a single write region. Waiting for a manual failover or turning regions read-only would defeat the availability benefit of multi-region writes.

questions.question: After a customer-managed (account) failover of a GRS storage account, the newly promoted primary region is automatically GRS-protected again, with no further configuration needed.
questions.explanation: Immediately after an account failover, the storage account becomes locally redundant in its new primary region until an administrator explicitly reconfigures geo-redundancy — that protection isn't restored automatically on its own.

questions.question: A SQL Server VM replicated with Site Recovery must fail over after a regional outage. The team would rather lose a few more minutes of data than start the database from a state captured mid-transaction. Which recovery point should they select when failing over?
options: Latest, which processes all data sent to Site Recovery for the lowest RPO
Latest app-consistent, captured with the application quiesced
A custom recovery point chosen from the crash-consistent points
Latest processed, which gives the lowest RTO
questions.explanation: The latest app-consistent point is the most recent one captured with the application quiesced, so no transaction is cut in half; the cost is a slightly older point because these are captured less often. Latest prioritizes the lowest RPO by processing everything received, but it does not guarantee application consistency. Latest processed prioritizes the lowest RTO by using the newest point already processed, again without that guarantee. A crash-consistent point captures the disk as if power had been lost, which is the mid-transaction risk the team wants to avoid.

questions.question: A company uses Traffic Manager to (1) send traffic to a disaster recovery region only when the primary region fails, and (2) keep European users on European endpoints for data-residency reasons. Which two routing methods meet these needs? (Choose two.)
options: Weighted routing
Geographic routing
Performance routing
Priority routing
MultiValue routing
questions.explanation: Priority routing sends traffic to the primary endpoint and moves to the next only when the first fails, which is the DNS-layer pattern for active-passive disaster recovery, and Geographic routing maps each user's location to defined endpoints, which is how data-residency rules are enforced. Performance routing picks the lowest-latency endpoint, which could send a European user to a non-European endpoint. Weighted routing splits traffic by ratio, and MultiValue returns several healthy IP addresses; neither expresses failover order or residency.

questions.question: An organization wants to apply the same Azure Policy assignments, RBAC roles, and Azure Monitor collection it uses for its Azure VMs to servers that will stay in its own datacenter indefinitely, on hardware it already owns. Which service should it use?
options: Azure Stack HCI clusters in the datacenter
Azure Arc-enabled servers
Azure Migrate with an on-premises appliance
Azure Lighthouse delegated resource management
questions.explanation: Arc-enabled servers project non-Azure machines as Azure resources, so Policy, RBAC, and Monitor apply without moving the workload or replacing the hardware. Azure Stack HCI is a hosting platform that runs on validated hardware, not a management layer for existing servers. Azure Migrate prepares workloads to move to Azure, which is not the plan. Lighthouse delegates management across Azure tenants and does not extend Azure management to machines outside Azure.

questions.question: A software company wants enterprise customers to reach its multi-tenant SaaS service privately from their own VNets, without traffic crossing the public internet. Customers' address spaces overlap with each other and with the company's. What should the company configure behind its service?
options: A public IP address with NSG rules scoped to each customer's range
Azure Private Link service, reached through customers' own private endpoints
A service endpoint on the subnet that hosts the company's service
VNet peering between the company's VNet and every customer's VNet
questions.explanation: Private Link service publishes the service behind a Standard Load Balancer, and each customer connects through a private endpoint whose address comes from the customer's own VNet; traffic is translated on the provider side, so overlapping address spaces do not matter. VNet peering cannot connect networks with overlapping address ranges and does not scale to many customers. A service endpoint only secures traffic from the company's own subnet to Azure PaaS services. A public IP with NSG rules still relies on a public endpoint.

questions.question: To expose an API Management instance to external partners, the instance must be deployed in external VNet mode, because an internal-mode instance cannot be reached from the internet.
questions.explanation: An internal-mode instance has only private endpoints, but it can still be published externally by placing an Application Gateway with a public frontend in front of it. That is a common pattern: the public entry point provides WAF and TLS handling while the API Management gateway itself stays private.

questions.question: Backend VMs behind a Basic load balancer (a SKU since retired) served public HTTP traffic with no NSG attached anywhere. After the team upgrades to a Standard load balancer and Standard public IP, clients can no longer reach the VMs, though the load-balancing rules are unchanged. What should you do?
options: Enable HA ports on the load-balancing rule to accept traffic on every port
Add the VMs' NICs to an application security group that names the web tier
Associate an NSG that allows inbound traffic on the application port
Add an outbound rule to the load balancer so return traffic is permitted
questions.explanation: The Standard SKU is closed to inbound traffic until an NSG explicitly allows it, whereas Basic accepted inbound traffic with no NSG at all, so associating an NSG with an allow rule for the application port restores access. An application security group is only a way to name groups of NICs inside NSG rules; without an NSG allow rule it permits nothing. Outbound rules govern SNAT for outbound connections, not inbound reachability. HA ports applies to internal load balancers and does not open anything.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure Arc are true? (Choose two.)
options: Arc-enabled servers must be migrated to Azure VMs before Azure Policy can be applied to them
Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters running outside Azure can be configured from Azure with GitOps
Arc requires a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute connection for its agent to reach Azure
Azure Policy guest configuration can assess the settings inside Arc-enabled servers
Arc can manage Windows Server machines but not Linux servers
questions.explanation: Arc extends Azure management to resources outside Azure: Kubernetes clusters can be configured declaratively with GitOps, and Policy guest configuration audits settings inside the OS of Arc-enabled servers. The Connected Machine agent needs only outbound HTTPS connectivity, optionally through Private Link, not a VPN or ExpressRoute link. Servers stay where they are, and Linux servers are supported alongside Windows Server.

questions.question: Resource logs from 40 Azure resources in three regions must be forwarded in near real time to a third-party SIEM that is hosted outside Azure and reads from Kafka-compatible or event hub endpoints. The same logs must also be queryable in Azure. What should you recommend?
options: An Azure Advisor export of the resource logs on a daily schedule
A diagnostic setting that sends the logs to a storage account, which the SIEM polls every hour
Azure Monitor Agent on each resource with a data collection rule that targets the SIEM
Diagnostic settings that send the logs to an event hub and to a Log Analytics workspace
questions.explanation: A diagnostic setting can send the same data to several destinations, and an event hub is the streaming destination that external SIEMs consume, while the workspace serves queries in Azure. A storage account is an archive that the SIEM would poll with delay. Azure Monitor Agent collects guest data from machines and does not apply to platform resource logs. Advisor produces recommendations, not logs.
questions.whyTested: Routing logs to the right destination is an explicit design skill: consumer and latency decide the destination.

questions.question: A security team ingests 2 TB per day of verbose firewall logs. They are rarely queried, but must be retained and searchable for 7 years for audits, and cost must be minimized. Which design is best?
options: Delete the logs after 30 days and rely on Microsoft Defender for Cloud to keep the history
Put the table on a low-cost table plan and extend its total retention to seven years
Send the logs to Application Insights, which keeps all telemetry for seven years
Keep the table on the Analytics plan and set interactive retention to seven years
questions.explanation: Table plans let rarely used, high-volume data sit on a cheaper plan, and total retention can be extended to up to 12 years, with older data retrieved by search jobs or queries as the plan allows. Keeping everything on the Analytics plan pays the full interactive price for data nobody queries. Application Insights has no seven-year guarantee, and Defender for Cloud does not keep your raw logs.

questions.question: An AKS platform team already uses PromQL queries and Grafana dashboards. It wants to keep them for new Azure clusters without running and patching Prometheus servers or Grafana instances. Which services should you recommend?
options: Azure Monitor managed Prometheus with Azure Managed Grafana
Application Insights with an availability test created for each pod
VM insights on each AKS node with the Dependency map switched on
Azure Service Health with a custom alert rule created per cluster
questions.explanation: Managed Prometheus stores the metrics without servers to operate, and Managed Grafana hosts the dashboards, so existing PromQL and Grafana skills transfer. Application Insights targets application telemetry, not pod metrics. VM insights looks at nodes as VMs, not Kubernetes workloads, and Service Health reports on Azure platform incidents.

questions.question: You are designing data collection for 300 Windows and Linux VMs, some Arc-enabled. Security events must go to one workspace, performance counters to another, and a noisy event ID must be dropped before storage to save cost. Which approach meets the requirements?
options: Diagnostic settings on each VM resource that filter out the noisy event ID before storage
The legacy Log Analytics agent with a single workspace key configured on each machine
Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules that route sources and transform rows
A custom script on every VM that deletes the noisy events from the workspace afterwards
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor Agent is the supported collector, and its data collection rules choose sources, destinations, and transformations, so different data can go to different workspaces and noisy rows can be dropped at ingestion. The legacy agent was retired in August 2024 and has no data collection rules. Diagnostic settings handle platform logs and not guest data, and deleting events afterwards means paying to ingest them first.

questions.question: Users report intermittent failures in a checkout flow that spans a web front end, three microservices, and a SQL database. You need to see end-to-end transaction traces and the slowest dependency. Which solution should you recommend?
options: Application Insights with distributed tracing across the services
VM insights with the Map feature enabled on all of the web servers
Azure Advisor performance recommendations reviewed for each service
Network Watcher connection monitor between each pair of services
questions.explanation: Application Insights follows a request across services and dependencies, which shows where time is spent. VM insights shows machine performance and connections but no application transactions. Advisor gives configuration recommendations and not traces, and connection monitor measures network latency, which does not reveal which application dependency is slow.

questions.question: VM1 stopped responding at 03:10. You need to know quickly whether the cause was an Azure platform event affecting that VM, such as a host failure, rather than something inside the guest. Which tool should you check first?
options: Azure Policy compliance for the resource group
Log Analytics workspace usage and cost
Azure Advisor reliability recommendations
Resource Health for VM1
questions.explanation: Resource Health reports the availability of an individual resource and whether a platform event, such as a host problem, affected it. Service Health is the subscription-wide view of incidents and maintenance. Advisor offers configuration suggestions, workspace usage is about cost, and Policy compliance does not report availability.

questions.question: Remote employees must reach an on-premises intranet web application from the internet. Security forbids opening inbound ports and prefers authentication before any traffic reaches the datacenter, with Conditional Access applied. There is no VPN. What should you recommend?
options: Microsoft Entra Domain Services with a secure LDAP endpoint
Microsoft Entra Application Proxy with a connector installed on-premises
A site-to-site VPN gateway and a public load balancer in front of the web servers
Azure Front Door with the on-premises servers as public origins
questions.explanation: Application Proxy uses an outbound-only connector, preauthenticates through Microsoft Entra ID, and can apply Conditional Access, with no inbound ports. A VPN and public load balancer expose more and are not preauthenticated. Front Door would need the servers reachable publicly, and Domain Services provides legacy domain features, not web publishing.

questions.question: A startup is designing a new consumer mobile app that needs sign-up, sign-in with social accounts, and self-service password reset, for an expected 30,000 monthly users. Which identity service should you recommend?
options: Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration invitations for each user
Microsoft Entra Domain Services with a custom login page
Azure AD B2C in a newly created tenant
Microsoft Entra External ID configured for customers
questions.explanation: External ID is the current customer identity offering and includes a free tier for the first 50,000 monthly active users. Azure AD B2C is no longer available for purchase by new customers, B2B invitations are for partner users in a workforce tenant, and Domain Services is not a consumer identity service.

questions.question: When an employee joins, the company must automatically generate a temporary access pass and add the person to the right groups on the start date, and on the last day disable the account. Which capability should you use?
options: Conditional Access with a sign-in frequency control
Privileged Identity Management with time-bound eligibility
Lifecycle workflows in Microsoft Entra ID Governance
Access reviews with auto-apply on a monthly schedule
questions.explanation: Lifecycle workflows run tasks for joiners, movers, and leavers on triggers such as a start date or last day. Access reviews recertify existing access periodically. Conditional Access governs sign-in conditions, and PIM governs activation of privileged roles.

questions.question: A data science team must read only the blobs that carry the tag Project=Cascade in a storage account that also holds data for other projects. You want to avoid creating a custom role or splitting the data into new accounts. What should you do?
options: Apply a CanNotDelete lock on every blob that carries one of the other tags
Assign Reader on the storage account and hand out a SAS token for each blob
Create a lifecycle management rule that deletes blobs which have other tags
Assign Storage Blob Data Reader with a condition on the blob index tag
questions.explanation: Azure ABAC adds a condition to a role assignment that checks attributes such as blob index tags, so the built-in role is narrowed without custom roles or new accounts. Reader is a control-plane role and SAS tokens per blob are unmanageable. Lifecycle rules and locks do not control who can read data.

questions.question: Regulators require that the organization's encryption keys are held in a single-tenant, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSM that the organization fully controls, and the keys will protect storage accounts through customer-managed keys. Which service should you recommend?
options: Azure Key Vault Premium with software-protected keys
Azure Key Vault Managed HSM
Azure Payment HSM
Azure Key Vault Standard
questions.explanation: Managed HSM is the single-tenant, fully managed HSM service on FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware, and it supports customer-managed keys for storage. Key Vault Standard keeps keys in software and Premium adds HSM protection in a multitenant service. Payment HSM serves payment PIN processing and is not a general service for storage encryption keys.

questions.question: An application running on VMs uses PKCS#11 to talk to an HSM today. The team plans a lift and shift to Azure with minimal code changes and needs a single-tenant HSM with PKCS#11, JCA, and CNG support. Which service fits?
options: Azure App Configuration
Azure Key Vault Standard
Azure Key Vault Managed HSM
Azure Cloud HSM
questions.explanation: Azure Cloud HSM is the single-tenant service with full native PKCS#11, JCA/JCE, and CNG support for lift-and-shift applications. Managed HSM and Key Vault are accessed through the Key Vault APIs, which would need code changes, and App Configuration does not store keys.

questions.question: Forty microservices read database connection strings and feature flags. Security requires secrets to live in a vault, developers want to toggle features without redeploying, and the same settings must vary by environment. Which combination should you recommend?
options: Azure Policy parameters that every application reads when it starts up
A storage account table that holds the secrets and the flags in plain text
App Configuration with labels and Key Vault references, using managed identities
Environment variables that are baked into every one of the container images
questions.explanation: App Configuration holds settings and feature flags centrally, uses labels per environment, references secrets in Key Vault so they are never stored in it, and lets applications refresh without redeploying. Baked-in variables require rebuilds, plain-text tables break the secrets requirement, and Policy parameters are governance inputs rather than runtime configuration.

questions.question: A company must discover and classify sensitive data across Azure SQL, storage accounts, and on-premises file servers, and show data lineage to auditors. Which service should you recommend?
options: Microsoft Purview
Azure Policy built-in initiatives
Microsoft Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance
Azure Resource Graph
questions.explanation: Purview catalogs and classifies data across sources and tracks lineage. Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance reports whether resource configuration meets a standard, Resource Graph queries resource metadata, and Policy enforces rules on resource properties; none of them classifies the content of data.

questions.question: Auditors ask you to show how the subscriptions currently measure up against the PCI DSS standard, with a list of failing controls and the resources involved. Which feature should you use?
options: A Log Analytics workbook showing the VM count per region
A management group with a CanNotDelete lock on every subscription
The regulatory compliance dashboard in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
The Azure Advisor cost recommendations list
questions.explanation: The regulatory compliance dashboard maps resource configuration to standards, including PCI DSS, through Azure Policy initiatives and lists failing controls with the affected resources. Resource counts, cost recommendations, and locks do not assess compliance with a standard.

questions.question: Every resource in the subscription must automatically receive the CostCenter tag from its resource group when the tag is missing, without developers adding it to templates. What should you assign?
options: A Deny policy that rejects any resource created without the CostCenter tag
A Modify policy that inherits the CostCenter tag from the resource group
A resource lock configured on each group to copy its tags to the resources
An Azure RBAC role that grants permission to write tags on all resources
questions.explanation: Tags are not inherited automatically, and a Modify policy, such as the built-in inherit-a-tag-from-the-resource-group policy, adds the missing tag to resources. Deny would block deployments rather than fix them, RBAC governs who can write tags and not what gets written, and locks do not copy tags.

questions.question: Which two statements about diagnostic settings are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A destination can be an event hub, which is how data is streamed to an external SIEM
A diagnostic setting collects guest operating system logs from inside a VM
One diagnostic setting can send the same data to a workspace and to a storage account
A diagnostic setting is the only way to configure alert rules on metrics
questions.explanation: A diagnostic setting routes platform resource logs and metrics to one or more destinations, including workspaces, storage accounts, event hubs, and partner solutions. Guest operating system data comes from Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule, and alert rules are separate resources from diagnostic settings.

questions.question: Azure AD B2C remains available for new customers to purchase, so it is the recommended identity service for a new consumer app designed today.
questions.explanation: Effective May 1, 2025, Azure AD B2C is no longer available to purchase for new customers, so new consumer identity designs use Microsoft Entra External ID. Existing B2C tenants keep working.

questions.question: A Log Analytics table's total retention can be extended well beyond its interactive retention, up to 12 years, so rarely used data can be kept at lower cost.
questions.explanation: Analytics retention keeps data fully available for interactive queries, and total retention can be extended to up to 12 years, with the older data in a low-cost state that is reached with search jobs for Analytics and Basic tables.

questions.question: A bank stores national ID numbers in an Azure SQL Database. Database administrators and Microsoft operators must not be able to read the plaintext values, yet an application must still query them with equality comparisons. Which feature should you recommend?
options: Transparent data encryption with a customer-managed key in Azure Key Vault
Always Encrypted, with the keys held in Azure Key Vault and used only by the client driver
Dynamic data masking on the column for all non-administrative users
Row-level security that filters rows by the signed-in user
questions.explanation: Always Encrypted encrypts the column on the client, so the database engine and its administrators only ever see ciphertext, while deterministic encryption allows equality lookups. TDE encrypts files at rest but the engine and administrators still read plaintext. Dynamic data masking only changes what query results display and does not stop privileged users, and row-level security restricts rows rather than hiding column values.
questions.whyTested: Data protection questions ask which feature stops which actor: stolen media, an administrator, or an ordinary user.

questions.question: Call-center agents query a customer table and must see only the last four digits of each credit card number, while the billing team sees the full number. The data must remain unchanged in storage. What should you configure?
options: A separate copy of the table where the card numbers are truncated by a nightly job
Always Encrypted on the card column with keys given only to the billing team
Transparent data encryption with separate keys for the two teams
Dynamic data masking on the card column, with the billing team granted the UNMASK permission
questions.explanation: Dynamic data masking changes what queries return for users without UNMASK, leaving stored data untouched, and it is simple to apply. Always Encrypted would also hide the value from agents but needs client driver changes and does not offer partial display. TDE has one key per database, not per team, and a nightly truncated copy is stale and doubles the data to manage.

questions.question: An auditor must be able to prove that rows in a financial table were not altered after they were written, even by a database administrator. Which Azure SQL feature should you recommend?
options: Row-level security that blocks updates for administrators
Ledger tables, with digests stored in a tamper-resistant location
Dynamic data masking on every financial column
Point-in-time restore with a seven-day retention
questions.explanation: Ledger makes data changes tamper-evident by chaining cryptographic hashes into digests that can be verified later, and the digests can be stored outside the database's control. Masking affects display, row-level security can be altered by someone with enough privilege, and point-in-time restore recovers earlier states but does not prove that nothing was altered.

questions.question: An OLTP database of 70 TB must stay on T-SQL. A reporting team needs several read-only replicas with their own compute size, isolated from the transactional workload, and backups must not slow the primary. Which design should you recommend?
options: Azure SQL Database Hyperscale with named replicas for the reporting workload
Azure SQL Database Business Critical with the built-in readable secondary
A General Purpose database with five geo-replicas in other regions
Azure SQL Managed Instance General Purpose with an elastic pool of replicas
questions.explanation: Hyperscale supports databases up to 128 TB, takes snapshot-based backups that do not load compute, and offers up to 30 named replicas, each with independently chosen compute for workload isolation. Business Critical has far lower size limits and only a built-in secondary. General Purpose cannot hold 70 TB, and elastic pools are not replicas of a single database.

questions.question: A development team's Azure SQL Database is used for a few hours on weekdays and is idle overnight and at weekends. Cost must be minimized, and a short delay on the first connection after idle time is acceptable. Which configuration should you recommend?
options: Hyperscale with the maximum number of named replicas
A DTU Premium database with reserved capacity
General Purpose serverless compute with auto-pause enabled
Business Critical provisioned compute with the smallest vCore count
questions.explanation: Serverless scales compute with usage, bills per second, and can pause when idle so that only storage is billed, and the first connection after a pause resumes the database after a delay. The other options bill for provisioned resources around the clock, and replicas or reservations add cost instead of removing it.

questions.question: A SaaS provider hosts 250 small Azure SQL databases, one per tenant. Each is busy at different times of the day, and per-database sizing wastes money. Which design provides the lowest cost without code changes?
options: Place the databases in an elastic pool sized for the combined peak
Move every tenant database to its own SQL Server on a virtual machine
Merge all tenants into one Hyperscale database and filter by tenant ID
Give every database a Business Critical provisioned size for its own peak
questions.explanation: An elastic pool lets databases share vCores or eDTUs, so tenants peaking at different times use the same pool without each being sized for its own peak. Merging tenants changes the application and the isolation model. Sizing each database for its peak is what wastes money, and a VM per tenant adds administration and cost.

questions.question: A company runs SQL Server 2022 on-premises. It wants near real-time replication to Azure SQL Managed Instance to run reporting there now, to migrate with minimal downtime later, and to be able to fail back to on-premises if needed. Which feature should you recommend?
options: Azure Database Migration Service in offline mode
Transactional replication with a distribution database on the managed instance
Log shipping to Azure Blob Storage with manual restore
The Managed Instance link feature
questions.explanation: The link uses distributed availability groups to replicate in near real time between SQL Server and Managed Instance, allows read-only offloading and migration, and with SQL Server 2022 supports failing back. Offline migration service runs are not continuous, and log shipping and transactional replication do not offer the same managed failover and failback.

questions.question: A retrieval-augmented generation application stores product documents as JSON in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL and needs similarity search over embeddings. The team wants to avoid running and syncing a separate vector database. What should you recommend?
options: Move the documents to Azure SQL Database and use Always Encrypted for similarity
Store the embeddings in the same containers and use Cosmos DB vector search with a DiskANN index
Export the documents to Azure Files and search them with grep from an AKS job
Copy the embeddings nightly into Azure Table Storage and query them there
questions.explanation: Cosmos DB for NoSQL supports vector embeddings next to the documents and similarity queries with flat, quantized flat, or DiskANN indexes, so no second system has to be kept in sync. Table Storage has no vector search, file search with grep does not scale, and Always Encrypted is a protection feature and not a similarity feature.

questions.question: A lift-and-shift of a Linux high-performance application requires NFS 4.1 volumes with very low latency, snapshots, and cross-region replication. The team wants a fully managed first-party service rather than building NFS servers on VMs. Which service should you recommend?
options: Azure Elastic SAN volumes exposed over iSCSI
Azure Blob Storage with the NFS 3.0 endpoint
Azure Files with a Standard HDD share
Azure NetApp Files
questions.explanation: Azure NetApp Files provides managed NFS and SMB volumes with high performance, snapshots, and cross-region replication. The NFS endpoint of Blob Storage is for object workloads and has different semantics. Elastic SAN is block storage over iSCSI, not a file system, and a Standard HDD Azure Files share cannot meet very low latency.

questions.question: A platform team runs 60 VMs and an AKS cluster, each with block storage needs that change often. They want to buy and manage one pool of capacity, IOPS, and throughput that all workloads attach to over iSCSI, rather than sizing 100 separate disks. Which service fits?
options: Azure Files Premium shares
Azure Blob Storage with hierarchical namespace
Azure Elastic SAN
Azure Premium SSD v2 managed disks
questions.explanation: Elastic SAN is a pooled block storage service whose volumes attach to many compute resources over iSCSI, and capacity and performance are scaled for the SAN as a whole. Managed disks are sized and billed individually, Azure Files exposes file shares, and Blob Storage is object storage.
