questions.question: A company wants one SaaS platform for data engineering, a lakehouse, warehousing, real-time analytics, and Power BI reporting, with all data stored in one logical lake in open format and little infrastructure to manage. Which service should you recommend?
options: Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pool only
Azure SQL Managed Instance with SSIS packages
Azure HDInsight clusters with Data Lake Storage Gen2
Microsoft Fabric with OneLake
questions.explanation: Fabric unifies those workloads in one SaaS experience on OneLake, which stores data in open Delta Parquet format. A dedicated SQL pool covers only warehousing, HDInsight is cluster-based and needs infrastructure management, and Managed Instance with SSIS covers relational and ETL needs but not the lakehouse and real-time parts.

questions.question: Telemetry from 50,000 devices arrives at Azure Event Hubs. You need continuous SQL-like queries with five-minute tumbling windows that write aggregates to Azure SQL Database, with no servers to manage. Which service should you recommend?
options: Azure Batch with a pool of low-priority nodes
Azure Stream Analytics
Azure Data Factory with a tumbling window trigger
An Azure Functions timer trigger that polls the event hub
questions.explanation: Stream Analytics is a managed engine for continuous queries with window functions over Event Hubs or IoT Hub streams and supports Azure SQL Database outputs. Data Factory schedules batch pipelines, a polling function must be coded and scaled by you, and Batch runs parallel compute jobs rather than streaming queries.

questions.question: A company will store about 200 TB of hot block blob data for the next three years, with a steady footprint. It wants to lower the cost per terabyte without changing the application or the redundancy. What should you do?
options: Switch the account from LRS to GRS
Enable blob versioning with a retention rule
Move all of the data to the Archive tier
Purchase Azure Storage reserved capacity for a three-year term
questions.explanation: Reserved capacity discounts a committed amount of storage for one or three years and suits a steady footprint, with no application change. Archive makes hot data unreadable until rehydrated, GRS raises the cost, and versioning keeps additional copies, which increases it.

questions.question: Archive documents must be protected against the loss of an entire Azure region with the highest durability available for Azure Storage, and read access during a regional outage without waiting for a failover is not required. Which redundancy option is the most cost-effective choice that meets the requirement?
options: Locally redundant storage
Zone-redundant storage
Geo-redundant storage
Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage
questions.explanation: Geo-redundant storage replicates data to a secondary region and offers at least 16 nines of durability, which satisfies protection against a regional loss. The read-access geo-zone variant costs more and adds capabilities that were not requested. ZRS and LRS keep all copies in one region.

questions.question: Which two statements about the Azure SQL Database Hyperscale service tier are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It is available in the DTU-based purchasing model as well as vCore
It supports up to 30 named replicas, each with its own compute size
Backups are taken by copying the whole database from the primary compute node
It supports databases up to 128 TB with storage that grows automatically
questions.explanation: Hyperscale offers named replicas for isolated read workloads and storage that scales automatically to 128 TB. It is available only in the vCore model, and its backups use storage snapshots that do not burden the compute node.

questions.question: Transparent data encryption protects the data of an Azure SQL Database from a database administrator who queries the tables, because the data is encrypted for them.
questions.explanation: Transparent data encryption protects data at rest in files and backups and is decrypted transparently for authorized sessions, so an administrator who can query the tables sees plaintext. Always Encrypted is the feature that hides values from administrators.

questions.question: Azure NetApp Files can present the same data over NFS and SMB in dual-protocol volumes.
questions.explanation: Azure NetApp Files supports NFS, SMB, and dual-protocol volumes, which makes it suitable for workloads that need the same files from Linux and Windows clients.

questions.question: A company stores 80 TB of business-critical documents in a Blob Storage account. Requirements: protect against accidental deletion of the whole storage account and against a malicious administrator, with a copy held outside the account. Which backup option should you recommend?
options: Blob versioning combined with a lifecycle management rule
Vaulted backup of the blobs to a Backup vault
Operational backup with point-in-time restore on the same account
Blob soft delete with a 365-day retention period
questions.explanation: Vaulted backup copies the data to a Backup vault in a separate, Microsoft-managed location, so it survives the deletion of the storage account. Operational backup, soft delete, and versioning all keep their data in the source account, so deleting the account removes them too, and lifecycle rules only move or delete data.
questions.whyTested: Recommending a backup for unstructured data hinges on where the protected copy lives.

questions.question: An Azure SQL Database must support restoring to any point in the last 14 days after user errors, and auditors require that the first full backup of each year is kept for 7 years. What should you configure?
options: Geo-replication to a second region, with the replica delayed by 14 days
Point-in-time restore retention of 7 years, with no long-term retention configured
An Azure Backup vault policy for the database with seven-year retention
PITR retention of 14 days plus long-term retention for yearly backups of 7 years
questions.explanation: Point-in-time restore retention is configurable from 1 to 35 days and covers the 14-day need, while long-term retention keeps selected full backups, such as a yearly one, for up to 10 years. PITR cannot be set to 7 years, geo-replication has no delay setting and is for availability, and Azure SQL Database backups are handled by the built-in features rather than a vault policy.

questions.question: An Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account must allow restoring a container to any second within the last 25 days after an accidental deletion. Which backup configuration meets the requirement at the lowest retention that satisfies it?
options: A Backup vault policy with daily recovery points
Continuous backup with the 30-day tier
Continuous backup with the 7-day tier
Periodic backup with the default interval and retention
questions.explanation: Continuous backup supports point-in-time restore to any timestamp within the retention tier, and the 30-day tier covers 25 days. The 7-day tier is too short. Periodic backup restores only to the stored snapshots, not to any second, and Cosmos DB is not protected by a Backup vault policy.

questions.question: Security wants assurance that even a compromised Global Administrator or backup administrator cannot disable immutability or delete recovery points in a Recovery Services vault before retention ends. What should you configure?
options: Enable the immutable vault setting and lock it so it cannot be reversed
Move the vault to a different resource group with a restricted RBAC assignment
Enable soft delete with the default 14-day retention only
Apply a CanNotDelete resource lock on the vault
questions.explanation: A locked immutable vault blocks operations that would lose recovery points and cannot be switched off, even by a privileged administrator. Soft delete alone can be disabled or changed, a resource lock can be removed by anyone with permission to delete locks, and moving the vault does not stop an administrator from acting on it.

questions.question: Deleting a protected item or disabling protection in a Recovery Services vault must require approval from a separate security team that the backup administrators cannot override. Which feature should you use?
options: Cross Region Restore enabled on the vault
A budget alert that notifies the security team of vault changes
Multi-user authorization with a Resource Guard owned by the security team
A custom Azure RBAC role that removes delete permissions from backup administrators
questions.explanation: Multi-user authorization protects critical operations with a Resource Guard that lives under the security team's control, so a second approval is needed. A custom role can be reassigned by whoever manages access, a budget alert has no relation to vault operations, and Cross Region Restore is a recovery feature in a secondary region.

questions.question: A company runs 120 on-premises VMware VMs. It has no secondary datacenter and needs a disaster recovery solution with an RTO of 30 minutes and an RPO of a few minutes, using Azure as the recovery site, with a tested plan that starts the database tier before the web tier. What should you recommend?
options: Azure Site Recovery with a replication appliance and recovery plans
Azure Migrate with a one-time replication and cutover
Azure Backup with the MARS agent installed in each VM
Azure Storage account with object replication enabled
questions.explanation: Site Recovery continuously replicates VMware VMs to Azure and uses recovery plans to order tiers and run test failovers. Azure Backup restores from copies and would not meet a 30-minute RTO for 120 VMs, Azure Migrate is for a one-time move, and object replication is a blob feature.

questions.question: A critical Azure SQL Database must keep running through the loss of a single availability zone, with automatic failover and no change to the application's connection string and no data loss, but the company does not need protection from a regional outage. What should you choose?
options: Place the database in an elastic pool with a higher vCore count
Schedule a nightly export of the database to a geo-redundant storage account
Configure an auto-failover group with a secondary in the paired region
Enable zone redundancy on the Business Critical or General Purpose database
questions.explanation: Zone redundancy keeps replicas or storage across zones in the same region and fails over automatically with the same connection endpoint. A failover group protects against a regional outage and involves another region, which was not requested. Exports are manual recovery, and a bigger pool adds capacity but no zone resilience.

questions.question: An Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server must tolerate the failure of its availability zone with automatic failover and zero data loss for committed transactions. Which setting provides this?
options: Geo-redundant backup with an automatic restore job
Zone-redundant high availability with a synchronously replicated standby
Same-zone high availability with a nightly backup
A read replica in the same zone that is promoted by a script
questions.explanation: Zone-redundant high availability keeps a standby in another zone, replicates synchronously, and fails over automatically. A read replica is asynchronous and promotion is manual, same-zone HA does not survive the loss of that zone, and geo-redundant backups restore with data loss and delay.

questions.question: A TCP-based game backend runs behind Standard public load balancers in East US and West Europe. Players need one static IP address, automatic routing to the closest healthy region, and fast failover, with client IP addresses preserved. Which service should you add?
options: Azure Application Gateway v2 deployed in each of the two regions
Azure Traffic Manager using the performance routing method
Azure Front Door Standard with both load balancers as origins
Global tier Azure Load Balancer above the regional ones
questions.explanation: The global load balancer provides a single static anycast IP address, geo-proximity routing to the closest healthy regional load balancer, and preserves client IPs for TCP and UDP traffic. Traffic Manager works at the DNS level and is subject to caching, Front Door and Application Gateway handle HTTP and HTTPS rather than arbitrary TCP.

questions.question: Three VMs run a stateless web tier in one datacenter, in a single availability set. The company needs the 99.99 percent VM SLA. What is the minimum change that achieves it?
options: Move the VMs to a larger size family with accelerated networking enabled on each NIC
Place all three VMs in a proximity placement group within the same datacenter
Deploy two or more VMs across zones behind a zone-redundant load balancer
Add two more VMs to the availability set and switch all of them to Premium SSD disks
questions.explanation: The 99.99 percent SLA requires two or more VMs deployed across availability zones, and a zone-redundant entry point avoids a single zonal dependency. An availability set offers 99.95 percent regardless of size or disks, and neither VM size nor proximity placement affects the SLA tier.

questions.question: A security architect wants one portal view that shows which VMs, databases, and file shares across 25 subscriptions are protected by backup or disaster recovery and which are not. Which should you use?
options: Azure Advisor cost recommendations
Log Analytics workbook for virtual machine inventory only
A Recovery Services vault in each subscription
Resiliency in Azure
questions.explanation: Resiliency in Azure, the new name of the Business Continuity Center, shows protected and unprotected resources across subscriptions and solutions in one place. Advisor cost recommendations do not measure protection, an inventory workbook does not know protection status, and individual vaults only see their own items.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure SQL Database backups are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Long-term retention can keep full backups for up to 10 years
Backups must be configured with a Recovery Services vault policy
Long-term retention keeps log backups so that any second can be restored for years
Point-in-time restore retention defaults to 7 days and can be set from 1 to 35 days
questions.explanation: Automated backups are on by default with a 7-day point-in-time retention that can be changed from 1 to 35 days, and long-term retention can keep full backups for up to 10 years. Long-term retention keeps full backups, not log backups, so it cannot restore to any second, and Azure SQL Database does not use a vault policy for these built-in backups.

questions.question: Operational backup for Azure Blob Storage protects data from the deletion of the storage account because the backup data is stored in a Backup vault.
questions.explanation: Operational backup is a continuous, local solution whose data stays inside the source storage account and is not transferred to the Backup vault. Vaulted backup copies data to a vault and protects against the loss of the account.

questions.question: A global tier Azure Load Balancer can distribute TCP and UDP traffic to the closest healthy regional load balancer and preserves the client IP address.
questions.explanation: The global tier uses a static anycast IP address, geo-proximity routing, and client IP preservation in front of regional Standard load balancers, and works for TCP and UDP traffic.

questions.question: A studio must render 40,000 independent frames every night within a few hours. The work is interruptible and each frame can be retried, and the team wants Azure to schedule tasks and scale the compute automatically at the lowest cost. What should you recommend?
options: An AKS cluster with a fixed set of on-demand nodes
Azure Batch with a pool of Spot VMs
A single large VM with a scheduled task
Azure Functions on the Consumption plan
questions.explanation: Batch manages pools, schedules tasks across nodes, scales automatically, and supports Spot VMs for interruptible work, which also lowers cost. One VM is neither scalable nor resilient, a fixed set of on-demand nodes wastes money and still needs a scheduler, and Functions has execution time and sizing limits that do not suit heavy rendering.

questions.question: A software vendor licenses a database engine per physical core and must guarantee that its VMs run only on servers dedicated to the company for compliance reasons. Which Azure compute option should you recommend?
options: Proximity placement groups
An availability set with five fault domains
Azure Spot Virtual Machines
Azure Dedicated Host
questions.explanation: Dedicated Host provides single-tenant physical servers, which supports per-core licensing and isolation requirements. Spot VMs run on spare capacity and can be evicted, proximity placement groups influence latency, and an availability set spreads VMs across racks without making them single-tenant.

questions.question: A healthcare company must run an application whose data stays encrypted in memory while being processed, so that even the cloud operator cannot read it. The application can run in a VM without code changes. Which solution should you recommend?
options: Azure Disk Encryption with BitLocker
Confidential VMs
Storage account infrastructure encryption
A VM with an Azure Hybrid Benefit license
questions.explanation: Confidential VMs run in a hardware-based trusted execution environment that protects data in use, with no application changes. Disk encryption and storage encryption protect data at rest, and a licensing benefit has nothing to do with data protection.

questions.question: A company must leave its datacenter in 10 weeks. It runs 800 VMware VMs with in-house tooling for vSphere, and the apps cannot be re-IP'd or re-platformed. Which target minimizes change and time?
options: Azure VMware Solution
Azure App Service Environment
Azure Virtual Machines after converting each disk to VHD
Azure Kubernetes Service with containers built for each app
questions.explanation: Azure VMware Solution runs the VMware stack on Azure bare metal, so VMs move with the same tools and without conversion or re-IP, which fits the deadline. Converting to native VMs, containerizing, or re-hosting as web apps all require change that the timeline and constraints rule out.

questions.question: A bank's internal web application must run in a dedicated, single-tenant App Service environment injected into its virtual network, reachable only privately, and scale to many instances. What should you use?
options: App Service Premium v3 plan with regional virtual network integration
Azure Container Instances in the virtual network
App Service Environment with Isolated v2 plans
Static Web Apps with a private endpoint
questions.explanation: An App Service Environment is deployed into your virtual network on dedicated infrastructure with the Isolated v2 tiers, giving the isolation and scale required. VNet integration only affects outbound calls from a multitenant plan, Container Instances is not App Service, and Static Web Apps hosts static front ends.

questions.question: A workflow integrating 30 SaaS systems must run inside a virtual network, have several workflows grouped in one app, and be developed locally by the integration team. Which hosting option should you recommend?
options: Logic Apps Standard
Logic Apps Consumption
Azure Data Factory with mapping data flows
Azure Functions Consumption plan
questions.explanation: Logic Apps Standard is single-tenant, supports virtual network integration, multiple workflows per app, and local development. Consumption is multitenant and pay per execution without those capabilities. A Consumption-plan function would need custom code for SaaS connectors, and Data Factory is a data integration service.

questions.question: An order-processing system must deliver messages in strict first-in-first-out order per customer, detect duplicate submissions automatically, and move poison messages to a dead-letter queue. Which messaging service should you recommend?
options: Azure Event Hubs with several partitions
Azure Event Grid custom topics
Azure Storage queues
Azure Service Bus queues with sessions
questions.explanation: Service Bus provides ordered delivery with sessions, duplicate detection, and dead-letter queues. Storage queues do not guarantee ordering or offer duplicate detection or a built-in dead-letter queue, Event Grid delivers discrete events with retries, and Event Hubs preserves order only within a partition and is a streaming service.

questions.question: Existing applications publish telemetry with Apache Kafka producers. The team wants to move to a managed Azure service with minimal code changes, and the data must also be archived automatically to Data Lake Storage. Which service should you choose?
options: Azure Service Bus Premium with topics
Azure Event Hubs with its Kafka endpoint and Capture
Azure Queue Storage with a function reading the queue
Azure Event Grid with MQTT topics
questions.explanation: Event Hubs exposes a Kafka-compatible endpoint so producers need little change, and Capture writes events to Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage automatically. Service Bus and Queue Storage are message brokers with different semantics, and Event Grid MQTT targets device messaging and discrete events rather than Kafka streams.

questions.question: An application sometimes calls a downstream service that is failing for minutes at a time. During those periods, the application's threads pile up waiting on timeouts and bring down unrelated features. Which design pattern should you apply to stop calls to the failing dependency?
options: Claim Check
Cache-Aside
Strangler Fig
Circuit Breaker
questions.explanation: A circuit breaker stops calls to a dependency that is failing and fails fast until it recovers, which protects other features. Cache-Aside improves read performance, Claim Check handles oversized messages, and Strangler Fig migrates a legacy system gradually.

questions.question: A web application reads product data from Azure SQL Database. Read load is high and the data changes rarely. You want to reduce database load and latency, accepting that entries must be rebuilt from the database if the cache is cleared. Which design should you recommend?
options: A second Azure SQL Database used as the system of record for reads
Azure Queue Storage in front of every read
Azure Managed Redis used with the cache-aside pattern
Azure Table Storage as the primary store for the products
questions.explanation: A cache using the cache-aside pattern holds frequently read data in memory and loads it from the database on a miss, which cuts latency and load. A second database adds cost and replication to manage, Table Storage as primary changes the data model, and a queue does not serve reads.

questions.question: A new design uses a caching tier. A colleague proposes Azure Cache for Redis Basic tier. Which is the best advice?
options: Use Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise, because that tier is supported for many more years
Use Azure Table Storage, because the Redis service has been retired for all tiers
Use the Basic tier, because it adds replication and zone redundancy at no extra cost
Use Azure Managed Redis, since the Basic tier retires on September 30, 2028
questions.explanation: Azure Managed Redis is the current offering for new designs, and the Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers of Azure Cache for Redis retire on September 30, 2028, while the Enterprise tiers retire on March 31, 2027. The Basic tier has no replication or zone redundancy, and Redis itself is available through Azure Managed Redis.

questions.question: A GitHub Actions workflow deploys Bicep files to Azure. Security forbids long-lived client secrets stored in the repository. What should you configure?
options: A personal access token of the lead developer stored in the pipeline
A federated credential on a managed identity or app registration using OpenID Connect
A storage account key stored as a repository secret
A service principal secret rotated manually every year
questions.explanation: Workload identity federation lets the workflow obtain tokens through OpenID Connect without stored secrets. A rotated service principal secret is still a stored secret, and account keys and personal tokens are broad, long-lived credentials tied to people or accounts.

questions.question: A company wants developers to self-serve complete test environments from templates, and proposes building the design on Azure Deployment Environments. What should you tell them?
options: It needs a Premium Azure DevOps license for each of the developers
It is available only in Azure Government and sovereign cloud regions
It is the recommended successor to Bicep for all new self-service environment designs
The service retires on 22 February 2027, so plan another approach
questions.explanation: Microsoft has announced that Azure Deployment Environments retires on 22 February 2027 and asks customers to transition to another Microsoft service, Azure service, or partner solution, so a new design should not depend on it. It is not a successor to Bicep and is not limited to Azure Government.

questions.question: Before migrating 600 on-premises servers, a company wants to discover them, map application dependencies, size the target VMs, and estimate Azure costs, without installing agents on VMware guests. What should you use?
options: Azure Arc-enabled servers
Azure Site Recovery replication appliance
Azure Migrate discovery and assessment with the appliance
Azure Backup Server
questions.explanation: Azure Migrate discovery and assessment uses an appliance to discover servers, supports agentless dependency analysis for VMware, and produces sizing and cost estimates. Site Recovery replicates for DR or migration but does not assess, Azure Backup Server backs up, and Arc projects servers into Azure for management.

questions.question: A company is moving a SQL Server instance that uses SQL Agent jobs and cross-database queries to a managed platform, and wants minimal downtime while the on-premises instance keeps running until cutover. Which migration path should you recommend?
options: Managed Instance with the Managed Instance link for replication
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, loaded with Data Factory pipelines
A single Azure SQL database, using a BACPAC export during a weekend window
SQL Server on a VM, using a nightly file copy of the data files
questions.explanation: Managed Instance supports SQL Agent and cross-database queries, and the link replicates in near real time so cutover is short. A single database does not support those features, a BACPAC means long downtime, and file copies and a NoSQL conversion do not meet the compatibility or downtime goals.

questions.question: A film archive must move 300 TB of files from a remote site with a 20 Mbps connection to Azure Storage as a one-time migration. Which option should you recommend?
options: Azure File Sync with a single server endpoint
AzCopy over the existing 20 Mbps connection
Azure Data Box appliances shipped to the site
Azure Storage Mover over the existing connection
questions.explanation: At 20 Mbps, 300 TB would take years to upload, so an offline appliance is appropriate, as Data Box suits data over about 40 TB with little network capacity. AzCopy and Storage Mover are online tools limited by the link, and File Sync keeps a file server in step over the network.

questions.question: An organization copies 8 TB of file shares from on-premises NAS devices and from an AWS S3 bucket to Azure Storage, with repeatable jobs and minimal downtime for the workloads, over a fast connection. Which service is built for this?
options: Azure Data Box Disk
Azure Storage Mover
Azure Site Recovery
Azure Import/Export with hard drives
questions.explanation: Storage Mover is a managed service for migrating files and folders from on-premises or AWS S3 to Azure Storage with minimal downtime and repeatable jobs. Data Box and drive shipping are offline methods that are not needed with a fast connection, and Site Recovery replicates VMs.

questions.question: A company protects 150 public IP addresses across several virtual networks. It wants DDoS rapid response support, cost protection for scale-out charges during an attack, and discounts on its Web Application Firewall. Which should you choose?
options: A network security group on each subnet
DDoS IP Protection on each public IP address
The basic DDoS infrastructure protection that every public IP gets
DDoS Network Protection on the virtual networks
questions.explanation: Network Protection includes rapid response support, cost protection, and WAF discounts, and covers many IPs in a virtual network, while IP Protection omits those features. Basic infrastructure protection offers no such extras, and an NSG is not a DDoS service.

questions.question: Two network virtual appliances in a hub exchange routes with Azure virtual networks. The team no longer wants to maintain user-defined routes by hand as spokes are added. Which service should you add?
options: ExpressRoute FastPath
Azure Route Server
Azure Firewall policy
A NAT gateway on the hub subnet
questions.explanation: Route Server exchanges routes between NVAs and the Azure network using BGP, so routes update dynamically. A firewall policy governs rules rather than routing, a NAT gateway provides outbound translation, and FastPath optimizes ExpressRoute data paths.

questions.question: An organization wants to restrict public network access to several storage accounts, Key Vaults, and SQL servers so that they accept traffic only from approved resources in the same boundary. The resources are not placed in virtual networks. Which feature should you use?
options: A network security perimeter
A network security group on a subnet
Azure Bastion
A route table with a default route
questions.explanation: A network security perimeter creates a logical boundary around PaaS resources outside virtual networks and controls their public access with inbound and outbound rules. NSGs and route tables apply to resources in virtual networks, and Bastion is for VM connectivity.

questions.question: A central network team must enforce that no virtual network in the organization allows inbound RDP from the internet, even if an application team creates an NSG rule that allows it. Which feature should you use?
options: Azure Policy with the Audit effect
Security admin rules in Azure Virtual Network Manager
A user-defined route to a null next hop
A network security group on each application subnet
questions.explanation: Security admin rules from Virtual Network Manager are evaluated before NSG rules, so a deny cannot be overridden by an application team's NSG. NSGs are owned by application teams, Audit only reports, and a null route breaks all traffic to the prefix rather than blocking one port.

questions.question: Latency-sensitive VMs in one region exchange many small packets and show jitter. The team wants to reduce latency and CPU overhead for networking without changing the application. What should you enable?
options: A NAT gateway on the subnet
Azure Front Door in front of the VMs
A larger NSG with more rules
Accelerated networking on the VM network interfaces
questions.explanation: Accelerated networking bypasses the host virtual switch, giving lower latency, less jitter, and lower CPU use. Front Door and NAT gateway do not affect VM-to-VM traffic inside the region, and more NSG rules do not improve performance.

questions.question: App Service back ends must accept traffic only from Azure Front Door over a private connection, with no public endpoint exposed. Which Front Door tier should you choose?
options: Azure Front Door Standard with origin IP restrictions
Azure Front Door Premium with Private Link to the origin
Azure Traffic Manager with a Priority profile
Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic)
questions.explanation: Front Door Premium supports Private Link connections to origins, so the origin can remain private. Standard can only restrict public access by header or IP, Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) retires on September 30, 2027 and is not the recommended basis for a new design, and Traffic Manager is a DNS service with no private connectivity.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure Batch are correct? (Choose two.)
options: There is no charge for Batch itself, only for the underlying compute and storage
Batch is a streaming engine for continuous SQL queries over events
Batch runs tasks on pools of compute nodes and can use Spot VMs
Batch requires every task to run on a dedicated physical host
questions.explanation: Batch schedules tasks across pools of nodes that can include Spot VMs, and you pay for the underlying resources, not for the service. Continuous SQL over streams is Stream Analytics, and tasks do not need dedicated physical hosts.

questions.question: Azure Storage queues are the best choice when messages must be delivered in guaranteed first-in-first-out order with automatic duplicate detection.
questions.explanation: Service Bus provides guaranteed FIFO ordering with sessions and automatic duplicate detection. Storage queues are simpler and cheaper but do not provide those guarantees.

questions.question: The Developer tier of Azure API Management is suitable for production workloads because it includes an SLA.
questions.explanation: The Developer tier is for non-production use and evaluation, and it does not offer an SLA. Production workloads use Basic, Standard, Premium, or one of the v2 tiers, or Consumption.

lessons.title: Identity & Access Management
lessons.summary: Hybrid sign-in methods, Conditional Access, just-in-time privileged access, and how standing access gets governed.
lessons.reading:
A design that touches identity almost always starts with how users actually sign in, and for an organization with an on-premises Active Directory, that means choosing among password hash sync, pass-through authentication, and federation. Password hash sync replicates a hash of each user's on-premises password hash up to Microsoft Entra ID, so sign-in keeps working even if on-premises infrastructure has a brief outage — Entra ID can validate the sign-in entirely on its own. Pass-through authentication instead validates every sign-in against on-premises Active Directory in real time through a lightweight agent, which means no password data is ever stored in the cloud, but it also means sign-in stops working if every authentication agent happens to be offline at once. Federation goes further still, handing authentication off entirely to an on-premises identity provider such as AD FS — useful when an organization has authentication requirements Entra ID can't satisfy on its own, at the cost of taking on and operating that federation infrastructure.

Once someone is authenticated, Conditional Access decides the conditions under which they're actually allowed to sign in — evaluating signals like the user, their device, their location, and a calculated risk score, then responding with a control. MFA is one of the controls Conditional Access can enforce, not a separate policy engine sitting next to it — a well-designed set of Conditional Access policies might require MFA only for risky sign-ins or unmanaged devices, rather than for absolutely everyone regardless of context. Because a Conditional Access misconfiguration could lock out every administrator at once, well-designed tenants also keep a small, tightly monitored emergency-access account, typically excluded from those same Conditional Access policies and protected by strong, ideally phishing-resistant credentials such as a FIDO2 passkey — not a security hole, but the one guaranteed way in if the main policies ever misfire.

Even with strong sign-in and Conditional Access controls in place, most organizations still don't want administrators walking around with permanent, standing access to privileged roles. Privileged Identity Management (PIM) solves that by making privileged role membership something you activate — just-in-time and time-bound, optionally requiring approval and a written justification — rather than something that sits active on an account all day, every day, whether or not it's actually being used. PIM and Conditional Access are commonly layered together, such as requiring MFA (a Conditional Access control) as a condition of actually activating a PIM-eligible role.

Standing access outside of privileged roles gets managed differently, and this is a common point of confusion on the exam. Access reviews periodically recertify access that already exists — an administrator, or the resource owner themselves, is prompted to confirm someone still needs what they already have, or to revoke it. Entitlement management works earlier in that lifecycle: it bundles resources into requestable access packages with an approval workflow and, critically, built-in automatic expiration for newly granted access. A scenario about giving contractors bundled, time-boxed access to a defined set of resources is describing entitlement management; a scenario about periodically re-certifying access someone already holds is describing access reviews.

Beyond sign-in, an architect also chooses how on-premises resources, customers, and secrets are handled. Microsoft Entra Application Proxy publishes internal web apps through an outbound-only connector with preauthentication, so no inbound firewall ports are opened. Microsoft Entra External ID covers partners and customer-facing apps, and replaces Azure AD B2C for new customers. Lifecycle workflows automate joiner, mover, and leaver tasks, and ABAC conditions narrow blob and queue data roles by attributes such as blob index tags.

For keys, Key Vault Standard or Premium covers most needs, Managed HSM is single-tenant on FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs for key sovereignty, and Cloud HSM serves lift-and-shift applications that need PKCS#11. Vaults should use Azure RBAC, managed identities, soft delete and purge protection, and private endpoints. App Configuration keeps non-secret settings and feature flags apart from code and can reference secrets in Key Vault.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to hybrid identity design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals:
Think of the three sign-in options like three ways a branch office checks a visitor's identity against headquarters. Password hash sync is like the branch keeping its own up-to-date copy of the approved-visitor list, so it can approve a visitor instantly even if the phone line to headquarters is briefly down. Pass-through authentication is like the branch calling headquarters for every single visitor in real time — nothing is stored locally, but the branch is stuck if that phone line ever goes fully dead. Federation is like refusing to keep any list at all and always redirecting the visitor to headquarters' own front desk to be checked in directly.

PIM works like a fire extinguisher kept in a locked cabinet: a powerful tool, but not just left lying on a table for anyone to pick up whenever — you break the glass, note why you're using it, and it goes right back afterward instead of staying in your hands indefinitely.
commonTraps: Pass-through authentication still calls back to on-premises Active Directory for every sign-in — it needs at least one authentication agent online, unlike password hash sync, which keeps working through a brief on-premises outage.

MFA is a control Conditional Access can enforce, not a separate policy system — a scenario needing MFA only under certain conditions is a Conditional Access design question, not a standalone MFA setting.
Privileged Identity Management doesn't replace Conditional Access — the two are commonly layered, such as requiring MFA to activate a PIM-eligible role.

A scenario about time-boxed, bundled access for contractors or a project team points to entitlement management; a scenario about periodically re-certifying access that already exists points to access reviews.
Azure AD B2C is not available to new customers; new consumer identity designs use Microsoft Entra External ID.
App Configuration holds settings and feature flags; secrets stay in Key Vault.
lessons.scenario: A multinational retailer has an on-premises Active Directory it isn't ready to retire, but wants Entra ID sign-in to survive a brief outage of its on-premises network. It deploys password hash sync rather than pass-through authentication, so authentication can complete entirely in Entra ID if the on-premises link drops. For its cloud administrators, it layers Conditional Access (requiring MFA and a compliant device) with Privileged Identity Management, so no one holds standing access to a privileged role, and activating one still has to satisfy that same Conditional Access policy. A small, tightly monitored emergency-access account is deliberately excluded from that policy, so a misconfiguration can never lock every administrator out at once. Finally, its quarterly compliance process uses access reviews to recertify who still needs standing subscription-level access, while a separate entitlement management access package handles the shorter-lived access each new contractor team needs for the length of their engagement.
lessons.onTheJob: In design review, the sign-in method conversation is really a negotiation about who owns risk during an outage — a client that's been burned by a WAN failure before will fight hard for password hash sync even when the security team's slide deck favors federation for its 'zero cloud password' feel. PIM sounds like pure security hygiene until an architect has to sell it to admins who've had standing access for a decade and treat activating a role every time as a productivity tax, so the real work is scoping which roles genuinely need it instead of adding friction nobody asked for. Access reviews and entitlement management rarely get built pre-emptively — they usually get retrofitted after an audit finding, which means the design that looks over-engineered in year one often looks exactly right by year three.

lessons.title: Governance, Policy & Monitoring at Scale
lessons.summary: Management groups and Azure Policy, landing zones and adoption frameworks, and designing Log Analytics and Azure Monitor for an enterprise.
lessons.reading:
At the largest scale, Azure's resource hierarchy exists so governance can be set once and inherit downward instead of being repeated everywhere. Management groups sit above subscriptions, letting an organization apply a single Azure Policy assignment or RBAC role once at the top and have it flow down to every subscription, resource group, and resource underneath — a conglomerate with independently run subsidiaries can still give each one its own policy and RBAC boundary at the subscription level while sharing a small set of mandatory controls, like required tags, applied once at a shared management group above them all. Azure Policy itself has several effects worth telling apart: Deny blocks a noncompliant resource from being created or updated at all; Audit flags noncompliant resources for visibility without blocking anything; and DeployIfNotExists actively remediates by deploying something like a missing diagnostic setting whenever a required one isn't already there. Only DeployIfNotExists and Modify can reach back and fix resources that are already noncompliant, by running a remediation task — Audit only reports on them, and Deny only stops new ones.

Rather than building this governance structure by hand for every new environment, Azure landing zones give an organization a pre-provisioned, consistent starting point — the management group hierarchy, policy assignments, identity foundations, and hub networking already built, so every new subscription lands into a governed environment from day one instead of each team configuring governance independently. Landing zones are the concrete, deployable implementation of the Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF), Microsoft's broader methodology for an organization's whole cloud journey — strategy, readiness, adoption, governance, and ongoing management. Where CAF and landing zones shape how an environment gets built, the Azure Well-Architected Framework shapes how any individual workload's design gets evaluated afterward, across five pillars: reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence, and performance efficiency. A lot of AZ-305 scenario questions are really asking which of those five pillars a particular requirement is prioritizing, since a design can rarely maximize all five pillars at once.

Monitoring an environment this size raises its own design question: whether to centralize every resource's telemetry into one Log Analytics workspace, or split it across several decentralized workspaces per team or subscription. A centralized workspace makes cross-resource queries and overall cost visibility simple, but gives everyone sharing it a coarser access boundary; decentralized workspaces give finer-grained access, retention, and data-sovereignty control at the cost of harder cross-workspace querying — a regulated subsidiary that needs its own retention period and access boundary is a strong signal for a dedicated workspace even inside an otherwise centralized design. None of this data shows up automatically, though: a diagnostic setting is the specific configuration on a resource that actually routes its platform logs and metrics to a destination, whether that's a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, or an Event Hub — without one configured, a resource's logs simply aren't being collected anywhere.

Once that telemetry is flowing, Azure Monitor splits it into two different tools suited to two different questions. Metrics are lightweight, numerical time-series data, well suited to fast, near-real-time alerting on something like CPU or memory crossing a threshold. Logs are detailed, structured or free-form records stored in that Log Analytics workspace and queried with KQL, suited to deep, multi-table investigation rather than an instant threshold check. Reaching for Logs when you need a fast, simple alert adds query latency you don't need; reaching for Metrics when you need a complex, correlated investigation doesn't give you the structure to support it. Two more tools round out ongoing governance at this scale: Azure Advisor analyzes what's actually deployed and how it's being used, then generates personalized recommendations organized by those same five Well-Architected pillars, while Azure Resource Graph queries resource metadata across many subscriptions at once with a Kusto-like query language — useful for auditing what's actually out there, even though, unlike Azure Policy, it doesn't enforce or remediate anything itself.

Choosing a logging design starts with the consumer. A diagnostic setting can send resource logs to a Log Analytics workspace for queries, a storage account for archive, and an event hub for streaming to an external SIEM, while Azure Monitor Agent and data collection rules gather guest data and can drop noisy rows before storage. Table plans and total retention of up to 12 years balance cost against query needs. For monitoring, Application Insights traces applications, managed Prometheus with Managed Grafana monitors Kubernetes, Resource Health reports on one resource, and Service Health reports platform incidents.

For governance, Microsoft Purview catalogs and classifies data, Defender for Cloud's regulatory compliance dashboard maps resource configuration to standards, and Azure Policy enforces rules. A small, enforced tag set, applied automatically with a Modify policy, supports cost allocation and inventory.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to org-wide governance design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of the management group hierarchy the way a franchise chain sets policy. Corporate sets a handful of non-negotiable rules once, at the top, and every franchise location inherits them automatically without corporate having to visit each location individually — while each location owner still runs their own day-to-day operations underneath that shared umbrella. A landing zone is like corporate handing a brand-new franchisee a fully built-out store, already up to code and already carrying the corporate signage, instead of making them build the whole space from an empty lot themselves.
commonTraps: Only DeployIfNotExists and Modify can fix existing noncompliant resources (through a remediation task) — Audit only reports on them, and Deny only blocks new ones from being created.
A landing zone is the deployable environment; the Cloud Adoption Framework is the broader strategy and methodology it implements — they aren't interchangeable terms for the same thing.
Reaching for Logs and KQL for a simple, fast threshold alert adds unnecessary query latency — that's what Metrics and alert rules are for.
A resource's logs aren't collected anywhere by default — a diagnostic setting has to be configured on that resource to actually send them to a destination.
A diagnostic setting handles platform resource logs; guest operating system data needs Azure Monitor Agent and a data collection rule.
Tags are not inherited; use a Modify policy to apply them automatically.
lessons.scenario: An enterprise with a regulated subsidiary is designing its Azure governance from scratch. It creates a management group hierarchy with a top-level group for company-wide policies (mandatory tagging, allowed regions) and deploys new subscriptions through a landing zone so every one starts with that governance, plus hub networking, already in place — following the Cloud Adoption Framework's broader guidance for how to sequence that rollout. Because the subsidiary has its own regulatory retention requirement, its subscription gets a dedicated Log Analytics workspace rather than joining the shared central one, with diagnostic settings configured on its resources to actually route logs there. Company-wide, a fast Metrics-based alert rule pages the on-call engineer within seconds of a VM's CPU spiking, while a deeper, KQL-based Logs query is used the next morning to investigate exactly what caused it — and Azure Advisor's recommendations, along with a Resource Graph query across every subscription, feed into the team's next quarterly review of the whole estate.
lessons.onTheJob: Getting a management group hierarchy and a mandatory tagging policy approved is often less about the technical design and more about which team loses autonomy — a subsidiary that's run its own subscription for years will resist inheriting central policy even when it's clearly the right call. Centralized versus decentralized Log Analytics workspaces is a fight that resurfaces every time a new regulated business unit joins the tenant, and the cheaper answer on paper often loses to a compliance team that won't accept sharing an access boundary. Landing zones sound like a one-time setup cost in a proposal, but in practice they quietly determine how painful every future workload onboarding will be, which is exactly why the upfront investment gets pushback before anyone's felt the payoff.

lessons.title: Data Storage Solutions
lessons.summary: Choosing a SQL hosting model, Cosmos DB consistency and partitioning, storage redundancy and access tiers, and moving data in and out securely.
lessons.reading:
Designing where a relational workload actually lives comes down to how much of the SQL Server engine you need versus how little you want to manage. Azure SQL Database, a single database, is fully managed platform-as-a-service with the least administrative overhead, but it doesn't expose every instance-level SQL Server feature. SQL Managed Instance sits in between: near-complete SQL Server engine compatibility, including SQL Agent jobs, cross-database queries, and linked servers, while staying fully managed PaaS. SQL Server running on a virtual machine gives full operating system and engine control for maximum compatibility, at the cost of patching and managing that OS yourself. A migration that depends on SQL Agent jobs or cross-database queries, but still wants to avoid managing the OS, points squarely at Managed Instance rather than Azure SQL Database.

For non-relational, globally distributed data, Cosmos DB exposes five consistency levels along a single spectrum, from Strong (no staleness, but the highest latency and lowest availability) down to Eventual (the lowest latency and highest availability, with no ordering guarantee at all) — Session, the default, fits most single-user scenarios where someone needs to see their own writes immediately, while Eventual fits read-heavy, shared workloads that can tolerate a few seconds of staleness for speed. Just as important as consistency is partition key design: a good partition key has high cardinality and spreads requests and storage evenly across physical partitions, while a low-cardinality key concentrates traffic onto a small number of partitions, creating a hot partition that throttles throughput no matter how much RU/s is provisioned. The fix for a hot partition is redesigning the partition key itself — raising the consistency level or adding more provisioned throughput doesn't touch the real problem.

Storage redundancy answers a different question: how many copies of your data exist, and how far apart are they? Locally-redundant storage (LRS) keeps three synchronous copies within one datacenter — the cheapest option, but it only survives a hardware-level failure. Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) spreads those synchronous copies across availability zones within the same region instead, surviving the loss of an entire datacenter without the cost or latency of replicating to a second region. Geo-redundant storage (GRS) asynchronously replicates to a paired secondary region, without any zone redundancy in the primary region itself, while geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) combines both — zone redundancy at home and geo-replication to a second region — for the strongest protection available. Only the read-access ("RA-") variants of GRS or GZRS actually let an application read from that secondary region before a real failover ever happens.

Everyday storage management layers a few more decisions on top. Access tiers trade storage cost against retrieval cost and speed: Hot suits data you touch constantly, at the highest storage cost and cheapest access; Cool and Cold suit infrequently accessed data; and Archive is the cheapest tier of all, but blobs have to be rehydrated, a process that can take hours, before they can be read again — the right pick when cost matters more than instant access, never when data needs to be readable at a moment's notice. For large-scale analytics, Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 is Blob storage with a hierarchical namespace turned on, giving engines like Synapse or Databricks POSIX-like access control and efficient directory-level operations instead of flat object storage. When it's time to actually migrate a database, the work splits into assessment and movement. The assessment step checks an on-premises database for compatibility issues before anything moves — historically the job of Data Migration Assistant (DMA), which Microsoft retired on 16 July 2025, with Azure Migrate and the SSMS migration component now covering that ground. Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) then performs the real migration, online or offline, once you're ready — assessment answers "will this break after we move it," and DMS is the service that actually moves it. And for reaching a PaaS data service privately, a private endpoint gives it a private IP address inside your VNet, reachable even from on-premises networks over ExpressRoute or a VPN, while a service endpoint keeps the public IP in place and only optimizes and restricts routing for traffic that already starts inside the VNet — only a private endpoint reaches a PaaS service privately from on-premises.

Protecting relational data means matching the feature to the threat: transparent data encryption for stolen files, Always Encrypted for an untrusted administrator, dynamic data masking for what users see, row-level security for which rows they see, and ledger for tamper evidence. For scale, elastic pools share resources across many databases, Hyperscale reaches 128 TB with up to 30 named replicas, serverless compute bills per second, and the Managed Instance link replicates in near real time from SQL Server. Cosmos DB for NoSQL can hold vector embeddings beside documents.

For unstructured and file data, choose between Blob and Data Lake Storage, Azure Files, Azure NetApp Files for enterprise file performance, and Elastic SAN for pooled iSCSI block storage. Analytics centers on Microsoft Fabric and OneLake, with Azure Databricks for Spark-heavy teams and Stream Analytics for continuous queries over event streams. Cost levers include tiers, lifecycle rules, and reserved capacity, and durability grows from at least 11 nines for LRS to 16 for geo-redundant options.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Azure data platform trade-offs? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Choosing between Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, and SQL Server on a VM is like choosing an apartment, a townhouse, or a standalone house: the apartment (Azure SQL Database) has the least upkeep but the least customization; the townhouse (Managed Instance) gives you more of your own space and rules while someone else still handles the roof and the plumbing; the house (a VM) gives total control, but you're the one calling a repair person, or being one, for every single thing that breaks. Storage redundancy is like deciding how many copies of your family photos to keep, and how far apart: one copy in a drawer (LRS) protects against a spill, copies split across two rooms of the same house (ZRS) protect against a room flooding, and a copy at a relative's house in another city (GRS/GZRS) is the only thing that survives the whole house burning down.
commonTraps: A hot partition is fixed by redesigning the partition key itself — raising the consistency level or adding more RU/s doesn't solve an uneven partition key.
Archive tier is the cheapest to store, but blobs need rehydration, which can take hours, before they're readable again — don't pick it for data that must be available instantly.
Plain GRS replicates to a secondary region, but that copy isn't readable until an actual failover — only the read-access (RA-) variants can be read from directly beforehand.
A service endpoint only optimizes traffic that already starts inside the VNet — reaching a PaaS resource privately from on-premises specifically requires a private endpoint.
Transparent data encryption does not hide data from a database administrator; Always Encrypted does.
Hyperscale exists only in the vCore purchasing model.
lessons.scenario: A healthcare analytics company is migrating an on-premises SQL Server database that relies on SQL Agent jobs and needs its Data Lake Storage Gen2 account reachable privately from its on-premises network over ExpressRoute. It runs a compatibility assessment first (through Azure Migrate), then targets SQL Managed Instance rather than Azure SQL Database, since Managed Instance supports SQL Agent jobs while still avoiding OS management, and uses Azure Database Migration Service for the actual online migration. For its Cosmos DB telemetry store, it redesigns a low-cardinality partition key that was creating a hot partition, and keeps Session consistency since each device needs to see its own latest writes immediately. Its storage account is configured for GZRS, protecting both against a single datacenter's loss and a full regional outage, with a lifecycle policy moving telemetry older than a year into Archive tier, and a private endpoint — not a service endpoint — providing the required private, on-premises reachability.
lessons.onTheJob: Choosing Managed Instance over Azure SQL Database because of SQL Agent jobs is a decision an architect often has to defend twice — once to a DBA team attached to its legacy tooling, and again to a finance stakeholder who sees the bigger line item and assumes it's over-engineering. GZRS and an Archive-tier lifecycle policy look great in a cost-optimization slide until a client remembers that rehydrating archived data takes hours, at which point the real conversation becomes what data can actually tolerate that delay versus what the business insists it can't. Partition key redesign for Cosmos DB is the kind of fix that's cheap on a whiteboard and genuinely painful in production, since it usually means a data migration the client didn't budget for when they signed off on the original design. A compatibility assessment that comes back clean is also not the same thing as a guaranteed-compatible migration — CLR assemblies, specific SQL Agent proxy accounts, and other instance-level quirks that assessment tools may not fully evaluate are exactly why a real proof-of-concept restore into a non-production Managed Instance is worth doing even after a spotless assessment.

lessons.title: Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery
lessons.summary: RTO/RPO-driven design, Azure Backup vs. Azure Site Recovery, availability zones vs. paired regions, and active-active vs. active-passive.
lessons.reading:
Every business continuity design should start from two numbers the business sets, not the other way around: RTO (recovery time objective), the maximum tolerable downtime, and RPO (recovery point objective), the maximum tolerable data loss. Only once those numbers are known does it make sense to pick a backup frequency, a replication approach, and how much failover automation to build — a design question that states specific RTO/RPO numbers is really asking for the cheapest architecture that still satisfies both, not the most impressive-sounding one available.

Two Azure services get confused constantly because they sound similar but protect against entirely different things. Azure Backup protects data: it restores a file, a VM, or a database to an earlier point in time, which is exactly what you want after accidental deletion or corruption. Azure Site Recovery protects availability instead, replicating an entire VM or workload to a secondary region or zone so it can fail over and keep running through an outage. A request to recover an accidentally deleted file points to Backup; a request to keep an application running after a whole region goes down points to Site Recovery. Both actually live inside the same Recovery Services vault, which stores backup data as well as Site Recovery's replication configuration and metadata — and it's easy to assume backups automatically survive a regional outage, when that actually depends entirely on the vault's own redundancy setting (LRS, GRS, or zone-redundant), which is worth checking explicitly rather than assuming.

Two different failure scopes call for two different tools working together, not one replacing the other. Availability zones give synchronous, low-latency redundancy across physically separate datacenters within a single region, protecting against the loss of one datacenter. A secondary region — paired with the primary — provides asynchronous disaster-recovery redundancy against a full regional disaster instead, at the cost of higher replication latency — a well-designed solution frequently uses both together rather than choosing one over the other. How a multi-region design actually behaves during a failure comes down to active-active versus active-passive: active-active runs full production traffic in two or more regions at once, giving the fastest possible recovery at the highest cost and complexity, including handling conflicting writes made in two places at once; active-passive keeps a warm or cold standby region that only takes over after a failover, cheaper but slower to recover. "Zero perceptible downtime during a regional failure" is the signal phrase for active-active; any standby that has to be activated first, warm or cold, is active-passive.

Some Azure services build failover automation in directly. Azure SQL Database auto-failover groups replicate one or more databases on a logical server to a secondary region and expose stable read-write and read-only listener endpoints that automatically redirect after a failover — so an application's connection string never has to change. That same read-only listener can actually serve reads from the secondary region even before any failover occurs, not only afterward, which is a detail worth remembering since it's easy to assume the secondary sits completely idle until disaster strikes.

Recovery design follows the data. Azure SQL Database has point-in-time restore (7 days by default, up to 35) and long-term retention up to 10 years, Cosmos DB has continuous backup in 7-, 30-, and 35-day tiers, and blobs have operational backup that stays in the account or vaulted backup that copies data to a Backup vault. Backups need their own protection: a locked immutable vault, enhanced soft delete, and multi-user authorization with a Resource Guard owned by a separate team. Site Recovery covers Azure, VMware, Hyper-V, and physical servers with recovery plans.

For high availability, two or more VMs across zones give a 99.99 percent SLA, and zone-redundant databases, flexible servers with zone-redundant HA, ZRS or GZRS storage, and multi-region Cosmos DB cover the data. The global tier of Azure Load Balancer fronts regional load balancers for TCP and UDP, and Resiliency in Azure shows protection across the estate.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to business continuity design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Backup is like keeping dated copies of an important document, so you can go back to yesterday's version if today's got corrupted or deleted — it fixes a data problem. Site Recovery is like having a fully-equipped second office ready to open immediately if your main building becomes unusable — not just a copy of your files, but an entire working replacement environment standing by, ready to actually run the business. Active-active is like already having both offices open and staffed every single day, so losing one changes nothing for customers; active-passive is like keeping the second office's lights off and unstaffed until the day you actually need to open its doors.
commonTraps: Backup restores a point-in-time copy of data; Site Recovery fails over an entire running workload to another region — they solve different problems and often coexist in the same design.
A Recovery Services vault's own storage redundancy setting determines whether backups survive a regional outage — don't assume they automatically do just because the vault exists.
"Zero perceptible downtime" during a regional failure describes active-active, not active-passive — any standby that must be activated first, warm or cold, is active-passive.
The read-only listener of an auto-failover group can already serve reads from the secondary region before any failover happens — the secondary isn't sitting completely idle.
Operational backup, soft delete, and versioning keep data in the source account, so deleting the account removes them too.
Zone redundancy handles a datacenter failure inside a region; a failover group or geo-replication handles the loss of a region.
lessons.scenario: A payments company sets its RTO at under two minutes and its RPO at near-zero for its core transaction database, and is willing to pay for the infrastructure that meets those numbers. It deploys Azure SQL Database with auto-failover groups across two regions in an active-active-leaning design, so the application's connection string never has to change during a failover, and configures its VM tier with availability zones for datacenter-level resilience plus Azure Site Recovery for full regional failover. Its nightly backups go to a Recovery Services vault explicitly configured for geo-redundant storage, since the original LRS default vault setting would have meant those backups couldn't survive the very regional outage the design is meant to withstand.
lessons.onTheJob: RTO and RPO numbers a client states in a workshop are often aspirational rather than actually costed out, so a real part of the job is translating 'we need near-zero downtime' into the dollar figure active-active multi-region actually costs, and watching how fast that appetite changes once the client sees it. Backup and Site Recovery get bundled into one line item in budget conversations even though they solve different problems, and the closest calls to a real incident are almost always the ones where a team assumed backups already survived a regional outage without ever checking the vault's own redundancy setting. Active-passive gets sold as basically the same as active-active for a fraction of the cost, which is true right up until an actual regional failure, when the failover time nobody stress-tested becomes the client's first real data point. Auto-failover groups also get quietly undermined by a shortcut: a developer who hardcodes the primary server's own connection string instead of the read-write listener endpoint will see everything work fine for months, right up until a real failover happens and that hardcoded string stops resolving to anything live.

lessons.title: Compute & Networking Architecture
lessons.summary: Choosing a compute service, hub-and-spoke topology, connecting networks together, distributing traffic, and filtering it.
lessons.reading:
Choosing compute for a new architecture is really a question of how much control you need against how much operational burden you're willing to take on. A virtual machine gives full operating system control, suited to legacy or highly specialized workloads that need it. App Service is managed platform-as-a-service web hosting with no orchestration layer to manage at all. AKS gives full Kubernetes control for complex microservices that genuinely need custom orchestration. Container Apps runs serverless containers with built-in, HTTP or event-based autoscaling and common microservices patterns, without you ever managing a cluster. And Functions is event-driven, per-execution billed compute, ideal for short-lived triggered code. "Wants container-based autoscaling but doesn't want to manage a cluster" is the classic signal pointing to Container Apps over AKS.

For networking at scale, a hub-and-spoke topology puts shared services — a firewall, a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, DNS — into a central hub VNet, while spoke VNets, one per workload or team, peer only to the hub and not to each other. That isolation is frequently the whole point of the design: by default, peering to a shared hub does not let two spokes talk to each other directly, and an Azure landing zone typically ships this topology already built for new workloads to land into. Connecting VNets and networks to each other has three main options, each solving a different problem. VNet peering connects Azure VNets directly over Microsoft's own backbone, with low latency and no gateway required. A Site-to-Site VPN Gateway connects an on-premises network to Azure over an encrypted tunnel across the public internet — cheaper and faster to stand up, but subject to internet variability. ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated circuit to Azure through a connectivity provider, bypassing the public internet entirely for the highest, most predictable bandwidth and latency, which is the answer whenever a scenario specifically calls for that predictability.

Distributing traffic across an architecture calls for a different service depending on scope and layer. Azure Front Door is a global, layer-7 entry point with edge caching and a Web Application Firewall, routing across regions. Application Gateway is a regional layer-7 load balancer, offering its own Web Application Firewall but only within one region. Traffic Manager is purely DNS-based global routing with no data-plane inspection at all — it only returns which endpoint's IP address a client should use next, so its failover is limited by client-side DNS caching (TTL), unlike Front Door's real data-plane failover. Filtering that traffic at the network layer has its own two-tier choice: a network security group (NSG) is a simple, free, per-subnet or per-NIC allow/deny filter on IP address, port, and protocol, while Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful, centralized firewall that also supports FQDN-based filtering and unified logging across many VNets — since NSGs have no concept of a fully qualified domain name, FQDN-based outbound filtering across a whole hub-and-spoke estate calls for Azure Firewall, not a pile of per-subnet NSGs.

Two more decisions round out this design space. Scaling an App Service plan up changes its pricing tier or size to a bigger instance; scaling out adds more instances of that same tier, often automated through autoscale rules based on metrics or a schedule — autoscale rules configure scaling out, never a tier change. And regardless of what gets built, Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — declarative ARM, Bicep, or Terraform templates that get version-controlled, reviewed, and deployed repeatably — is how a design requiring consistent, repeatable, auditable deployments across multiple environments actually gets delivered, instead of manually clicking through the portal each time.

More compute choices come from specific requirements. Azure Batch runs parallel jobs on pools that can use Spot VMs, Dedicated Host gives single-tenant physical servers, confidential VMs protect data in use, Azure VMware Solution moves a vSphere estate quickly, App Service Environment gives single-tenant web hosting inside your virtual network, and Logic Apps Standard runs single-tenant workflows.

On the network side, DDoS Network Protection adds rapid response and cost protection over IP Protection, Route Server exchanges routes with appliances using BGP, a network security perimeter controls public access to PaaS resources, and Virtual Network Manager can apply security admin rules that are evaluated before NSG rules. Accelerated networking and proximity placement groups reduce latency inside a region, and Front Door Premium adds Private Link origins and bot protection.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Azure compute and networking trade-offs? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Choosing a compute option is like choosing how much of a meal to cook yourself: a VM is buying raw ingredients and cooking entirely from scratch, App Service is a meal kit where the basics are already handled, and Functions is ordering delivery — you specify what you want and it just appears, with none of the kitchen work on your end. A hub-and-spoke network is like an office building with a shared reception desk and security team in the lobby (the hub), while each floor (a spoke) runs its own business independently — floors don't get to walk straight into each other, they all funnel back through that shared lobby first.
commonTraps: Container Apps adds built-in autoscaling without you managing a cluster — AKS is the one that hands you full cluster control (and full cluster responsibility).
VNet peering isn't transitive: peering A to B and B to C doesn't let A and C talk to each other without their own direct peering.
Traffic Manager only makes DNS-layer decisions — it never inspects or proxies the actual HTTP traffic the way Front Door or Application Gateway do.
NSGs have no concept of an FQDN — centralized, FQDN-based outbound filtering across a hub-and-spoke estate needs Azure Firewall, not more NSG rules.
A network security perimeter governs public access to PaaS resources; a private endpoint brings a service into a virtual network.
Front Door Private Link origins need the Premium tier.
lessons.scenario: A retailer is redesigning its Azure networking and compute footprint. It builds a hub-and-spoke topology, with Azure Firewall in the hub doing FQDN-based outbound filtering that individual NSGs in each spoke can't provide, and an ExpressRoute circuit connecting the hub back to its on-premises datacenter for predictable, high-bandwidth traffic. Its new checkout microservices go into Container Apps, since the team wants built-in autoscaling under Black Friday traffic without taking on cluster management, while a legacy inventory system that needs full OS access stays on a VM. Globally, Azure Front Door sits in front of the whole storefront, caching static assets at the edge and enforcing a Web Application Firewall across every region — deliberately not Traffic Manager, since the retailer specifically needs real content-aware routing and failover, not just a DNS answer. Every piece of this — the hub, the spokes, the firewall rules, the Front Door configuration — is deployed through Bicep templates checked into source control, so the whole environment can be rebuilt consistently in a new region if it ever needs to be.
lessons.onTheJob: Container Apps versus AKS is as much an organizational-maturity question as a technical one — a team pushing for AKS because it's what they already know is a common design-review fight, and the architect's real job is separating 'we genuinely need custom orchestration' from 'we don't want to learn something new.' ExpressRoute gets proposed constantly for its predictable latency, right up until procurement sees the monthly cost and asks whether a Site-to-Site VPN would really be that much worse — a question that usually has a real, testable answer instead of a gut-feel one. Azure Firewall's FQDN filtering sounds like nice-to-have governance in a proposal, but it becomes the thing everyone's grateful for the day someone has to reconstruct what an entire hub-and-spoke estate's outbound traffic rules actually allow. The Infrastructure as Code (IaC) discipline that closes out this design — version-controlled Bicep or Terraform instead of manual portal clicks — is the reason a hub-and-spoke estate built this way can actually be torn down and rebuilt in a new region on demand, rather than existing only as institutional memory of what someone once clicked.

lessons.title: Migration, Messaging & Integration
lessons.summary: Discovering and assessing workloads before a move, choosing the right messaging service, exposing and orchestrating APIs, and troubleshooting the network afterward.
lessons.reading:
Before any large migration begins, Azure Migrate serves as the hub for discovery and assessment — finding on-premises servers and workloads, right-sizing them, checking readiness, and estimating cost, all before a single workload actually moves. The real data migration itself is often handed off afterward to a more specialized tool, like Database Migration Service for a database, once Azure Migrate's assessment says a workload is actually ready to go.

Once workloads are in Azure, connecting them together calls for the right messaging or eventing service, and these three get mixed up constantly. Service Bus is a message broker built for ordered, transactional, point-to-point or publish/subscribe messaging with guaranteed delivery — the right choice when an order has to be processed exactly once, in order. Event Grid is a lightweight, reactive eventing service for discrete event notifications with push-based routing, suited to reacting to something like "a blob was created" rather than processing a queue of work.
